But when more and more CO2 is in the air, it gets warmer. CO2 contributes most to **human-caused warming**, because humans emit a great deal of it and it stays in the atmosphere for a very long time.

Around 1750 the air contained about **280 ppm** of CO2. Since **industrialisation**, people have been burning a lot of **coal**, **oil** and **natural gas**. CO2 is produced in the process. A lot of CO2 also gets into the air when forests are cleared. In 2024 the value was over **420 ppm**. On the volcano **Mauna Loa** in Hawaii the CO2 content has been measured exactly since 1958.

The bubbles in mineral water and lemonade are CO2, which in everyday speech is called carbonation (in German “Kohlensäure”, literally “carbonic acid”). Frozen CO2 is called **dry ice**. It is about minus 78 degrees cold and turns directly into gas without first becoming liquid. Fire extinguishers with CO2 smother flames because they displace the oxygen.

gewusst: Dry ice does not melt into a puddle, but turns directly into gas.
The series of measurements from Mauna Loa is called the **Keeling Curve** after its founder.

teile.einleitung: Moscow is the capital of Russia and one of the biggest cities in Europe. Well known are the Kremlin, Red Square with the colourful St Basil's Cathedral, and the magnificent metro.
wichtigste: Moscow lies on the River Moskva, after which the city is named.
In the Kremlin, an old fortress complex, the Russian president has his official seat.
Right next to the Kremlin lies Red Square.
St Basil's Cathedral with its colourful onion domes is a landmark of Russia.
The Moscow Metro is known for its splendid stations.
From 1712 to 1918 Saint Petersburg was the capital, and then Moscow again.

abschnitte.text: Moscow lies in the west of Russia on the River **Moskva**, after which the city is named. The Moskva later flows into the Oka, a tributary of the Volga. The city was first mentioned in writing in the year 1147. Today more than twelve million people live there. Moscow is the political, economic and cultural centre of Russia.

The **Kremlin** is a medieval fortress with high red walls, towers, palaces and churches. It is the official seat of the Russian president. On the east wall of the Kremlin lies **Red Square**. Its name has nothing to do with the colour: the old Russian word for “red” also meant “beautiful”. On the square stands **St Basil's Cathedral**, which was built in the 16th century under Tsar Ivan the Terrible. Its coloured onion domes are known all over the world.

The **Moscow Metro** opened in 1935. Many stations are decorated with marble, mosaics, statues and chandeliers. That is why they are often called “underground palaces”. The metro is one of the most heavily used underground networks in the world. Every day millions of people ride it to work or school.

**Lomonosov University** was founded in 1755 and is the best-known university in Russia. Its main building is one of the seven **Stalin skyscrapers**, mighty towers in the style of the 1950s. The **Bolshoi Theatre** is also world famous for ballet and opera. There are also many museums, such as the Tretyakov Gallery with Russian art.

For a long time Moscow was the capital of the Russian tsarist empire. In 1712 Tsar Peter the Great moved the capital to **Saint Petersburg**, which today is the second biggest city in Russia. In 1812 the French emperor Napoleon marched into Moscow, and a great fire destroyed large parts of the city. In 1918 Moscow became the capital again. Later it was also the capital of the Soviet Union.

gewusst: In the Kremlin stands the Tsar Bell, one of the biggest bells in the world, which has never been rung.
The Ostankino Tower in Moscow is over 500 metres high.

teile.einleitung: The Korean Demilitarised Zone, DMZ for short, separates North Korea and South Korea. It arose in 1953 with the armistice in the Korean War. To this day there is no peace treaty, and Switzerland too helps to monitor the armistice.
wichtigste: The armistice agreement of the Korean War was signed on 27 July 1953.
A peace treaty was never concluded.
The DMZ runs about 250 kilometres across the Korean Peninsula.
It follows the front line of 1953 and not exactly the 38th parallel.
In Panmunjom, meetings between the two sides still take place to this day.
Switzerland and Sweden have monitored the armistice since 1953.
Because hardly anyone goes in, the DMZ is a refuge for nature.

abschnitte.text: From 1950 to 1953 the **Korean War** raged between North and South Korea, supported by other states. On **27 July 1953** an **armistice agreement** was signed. It ended the fighting. A **peace treaty**, however, was never concluded. Formally there is therefore still no peace between the two states today.

The **Demilitarised Zone** is about **250 kilometres** long. It runs from the mouth of the **Han River** in the west to the east coast. In its middle runs the **Military Demarcation Line**, the actual border. The zone does not follow exactly the 38th parallel, but the **front line** of 1953. “Demilitarised” means that no troops are supposed to be stationed there. On both sides of it, however, the border is very heavily guarded.

In the village of **Panmunjom** on the demarcation line the armistice was signed. There lies the **Joint Security Area**, in which soldiers of both sides stand directly facing each other. In blue huts talks take place. In 2018 the heads of state **Kim Jong-un** from the north and **Moon Jae-in** from the south met here.

The **Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission** monitors whether the armistice is being observed. **Switzerland** and **Sweden** are represented on it. Members of the Swiss Armed Forces have been stationed in Panmunjom since 1953. This is one of the oldest peace-support missions of the Swiss Armed Forces.

abschnitte.titel: Dispute at sea and on land
abschnitte.text: The agreement did not settle the **sea border**. In the **Yellow Sea** the UN side drew the **Northern Limit Line**, which North Korea does not recognise. There clashes occurred several times, for example in 2010 at the island of **Yeonpyeong**. Near the border also lay the **Kaesong Industrial Region**. There North Korean employees worked for South Korean firms. South Korea stopped the project in 2016 after a North Korean nuclear test.

gewusst: Because the DMZ has hardly been entered since 1953, rare animals such as cranes live there.
The DMZ is a nature reserve that nobody planned.

teile.einleitung: The Mapuche are an Indigenous people in the south of South America. They are the biggest Indigenous people in Chile and also live in Argentina.
wichtigste: The Mapuche are the biggest Indigenous people in Chile.
They live mainly in the south of Chile and in Argentina.
The name means “people of the earth”.
Their language is called Mapudungun.
They successfully resisted the Spanish conquerors for a long time.

abschnitte.text: The **Mapuche** live mainly in the south of **Chile** and in the west of **Argentina**. Their name means “people of the earth”. The connection to the land and to nature is very important for their culture. Their own language is called **Mapudungun**. Today many Mapuche also live in cities such as Santiago de Chile.

When the **Spanish** conquered Chile in the 16th century, the Mapuche resisted successfully for a long time. Over many generations they were able to keep a large area south of the **Biobío** River independent. Only in the 19th century did the states of Chile and Argentina occupy their land by force.

Many Mapuche today demand that their land and their rights be recognised. This is much debated in Chile, and there are different opinions about it. At the same time, many Mapuche look after their **language**, their music and their festivals so that the culture stays alive.

gewusst: After the arrival of the Spanish, the Mapuche remained independent in a large area for about three centuries.

teile.einleitung: La Paz is the seat of government of Bolivia in South America. The city lies at about 3,600 metres above sea level, which makes it the highest seat of government in the world.
wichtigste: La Paz is the seat of government of Bolivia.
The city lies at about 3,600 metres in a basin in the Andes.
No other seat of government in the world lies so high.
According to the constitution, the capital is Sucre.
A large cable car network links La Paz with the neighbouring city of El Alto.
The snow-capped mountain Illimani rises above the city.

abschnitte.text: La Paz lies in a deep **basin** in the **Andes**. The houses climb up the steep slopes. The centre lies at about **3,600 metres**, which is higher than almost all the peaks of the Swiss Prealps. Above the city rises the mighty, snow-capped mountain **Illimani**. Above the basin, at about 4,000 metres, lies the large neighbouring city of **El Alto**.

abschnitte.titel: Seat of government, but not the capital
abschnitte.text: Bolivia has a special feature: according to the constitution, **Sucre** is the capital. The highest court sits there. The government and Parliament, however, work in **La Paz**. That is why La Paz is called the **seat of government**. The city was founded in the 16th century by the Spanish. Its name means “peace”.

Because the streets are steep and often jammed with traffic, La Paz has built a large **cable car network**. It is called **Mi Teleférico** and opened in 2014. The colourful lines link the districts in the valley with El Alto. For many people the cable car is now a completely normal way of getting about, just as buses or trams are elsewhere.

At great heights the **air is thinner**. With every breath it contains less oxygen. Many visitors therefore get a headache at first or tire quickly, which is called **altitude sickness**. The body gets used to it after a few days, though. Football teams from the lowlands often struggle in La Paz because they run out of breath more quickly.

gewusst: Lake Titicaca, one of the highest large lakes in the world, lies not far from La Paz.
Mi Teleférico is regarded as one of the biggest urban cable car networks in the world.

teile.einleitung: Migration means that people change their place of residence for a long time or for good. Some move within their country, others move to another country. Migration has existed as long as there have been humans, and Switzerland, too, has been shaped by immigration and emigration.
wichtigste: Migration is the movement of people to a new place of residence.
Movement within one state is called internal migration.
War in the country of origin is a typical push factor that drives people to leave.
Money that migrants send home is called remittances.
Brain drain means that well-trained specialists leave a country.
The UN refugee agency UNHCR has its headquarters in Geneva.
In Switzerland at the end of 2024, about a quarter of the permanent resident population did not have a Swiss passport.

abschnitte.text: The word **migration** comes from the Latin “migrare”, which means to move. Someone who moves to another country is an immigrant for that country and an emigrant for their country of origin. When people move within a country, for example from a village to a city, this is called **internal migration**. In 2020, about 280 million people worldwide lived outside their country of birth.

Researchers distinguish between reasons that drive people away and reasons that attract them. **Push factors** are, for example, war, persecution, poverty or natural disasters in the country of origin. **Pull factors** are, for example, work, safety, good schools or family in the destination country. Usually several reasons work together.

Some people have to leave their homeland because their lives are in danger. They count as **refugees** and are under the protection of international agreements. The UNHCR, which was founded in 1950 and has its seat in Geneva, helps refugees all over the world. According to the UN, in 2024 more than 100 million people worldwide were displaced, many of them within their own country.

abschnitte.titel: Consequences for the countries of origin
abschnitte.text: Many migrants send money back to their families. These **remittances** are a very important source of income for some poorer countries. But when many doctors, engineers or teachers emigrate, they are missing at home. This is called **brain drain**.

In the 19th century many Swiss people emigrated to America out of poverty. After the Second World War, Switzerland brought in many workers from Italy, later also from Spain, Portugal and the former Yugoslavia. Under the **seasonal worker status**, many of them were allowed to stay only for a few months and could not bring their families. This rule was abolished in 2002 with the free movement of persons with the EU.

When people from different countries live together, they bring languages, food, festivals and ideas with them. For living together to work, **integration**, that is, settling in on both sides, and respect are important. This includes, for example, learning the language of the new place of residence. Many Swiss customs and dishes, such as pizza, have become at home here through migration.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reason that makes people leave their homeland.
A reason that makes another country or place attractive.
Newcomers settling in and taking part in the new society.
When many well-trained people leave a country.
In the past, a foreign worker who was allowed to work in Switzerland for one season only.

gewusst: Swiss people also founded places abroad, for example Nova Friburgo in Brazil in 1819.
Besides the UNHCR, the International Organization for Migration also has its seat in Geneva.
Animals migrate too, but for humans, migration means a change of residence.

teile.einleitung: Lebanon is a small country in the Middle East on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean. It is known for its mountains, the cedar and a very long history.
wichtigste: The capital of Lebanon is Beirut.
A green cedar is shown on the flag.
Lebanon is about a quarter as big as Switzerland.
In ancient times the Phoenicians lived on the coast.
The fertile Beqaa Valley lies between two mountain ranges.
Lebanon used to be called the “Switzerland of the Middle East”.

abschnitte.text: Lebanon borders Syria and Israel and lies on the **Mediterranean**. The capital, **Beirut**, lies on the coast and is the country's biggest city. At about 10,450 square kilometres, Lebanon is about **a quarter as big as Switzerland**. The official language is Arabic, and many people also speak French or English.

Running parallel to the coast is the **Mount Lebanon range**, and in the east on the border with Syria the **Anti-Lebanon**. Between the two ranges lies the fertile **Beqaa Valley**. Grain, vegetables and wine are grown there. In winter there is often snow on the mountains, and you can even go skiing there.

The **Lebanon cedar** grows in the mountains and has been a symbol of the country since ancient times. Its wood was already in great demand in antiquity, for example for ships and temples. Today only a few old cedar forests are left. A green cedar can be seen in the middle of the **flag**, between two red stripes.

In ancient times the **Phoenicians** lived on the coast. They were a well-known seafaring and trading people. They founded cities such as **Tyre**, **Sidon** and **Byblos** and traded all around the Mediterranean. The Phoenicians developed an alphabet, from which many other alphabets later arose.

Because of its snowy mountains and the strong **banking centre of Beirut**, Lebanon used to be called the “Switzerland of the Middle East”. Many different **religious communities** live in the country, mainly Muslims and Christians. From 1975 to 1990 the country suffered a **civil war**. There have been political and economic crises again and again since then, too.

gewusst: Byblos in Lebanon is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
The word “Bible” goes back to the name of the city of Byblos, which traded in papyrus.

teile.einleitung: In salmon farming, salmon are not caught in the sea but raised in large farms. A large part of the salmon in our shops comes from such farms.
wichtigste: Most salmon sold in shops come from farms.
The fish farmed most is the Atlantic salmon.
Norway is the biggest salmon producer in the world.
The fish grow up in net pens in the sea, for example in the fjords.
Problems include sea lice and farmed fish that escape.
In Switzerland, too, there is salmon farming in indoor facilities on land.

abschnitte.text: In the wild, salmon live first in **fresh water** and later migrate to the sea. Farming copies this. The young salmon first grow up in tanks of fresh water on land. After that they are moved to large **net pens** in the sea. There they are fed until they are big enough. The fish farmed most is the **Atlantic salmon**.

**Norway** is the biggest salmon producer in the world. In the sheltered **fjords** along its long coast there are countless net pens. The cold, clean seawater suits the salmon well. **Chile**, Scotland and the Faroe Islands also farm a lot of salmon. A large part of it is sold to other countries, including Switzerland.

Farmed salmon are given feed made of fishmeal, fish oil and plants such as soya or rapeseed. Wild salmon eat small **crustaceans** that contain a red pigment. This gives their flesh its typical pink colour. That is why a pigment called **astaxanthin** is also mixed into the feed for farmed fish.

Where many fish live close together, diseases and **sea lice** spread easily. These small crustaceans attach themselves to the skin of the fish. Farmed salmon that escape can mix with wild salmon. In addition, leftover feed and droppings end up in the sea. That is why new kinds of farms are being developed, for example closed tanks. In Switzerland, there has been a salmon farm in indoor facilities on land for some years, for example in the **Grisons**.

gewusst: In the wild, a salmon often finds its way back to spawn in the river where it hatched.
In the past, many wild salmon also lived in the Rhine as far as Basel.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is warming more than the Earth on average. You can see this especially in the glaciers, which are shrinking fast. Experts at MeteoSwiss and the glacier monitoring network GLAMOS observe these changes closely.
wichtigste: According to MeteoSwiss, Switzerland has become about 2.9 °C warmer since pre-industrial times (as of 2025).
Worldwide the warming is about 1.3 °C, so Switzerland is warming about twice as much.
Land areas warm more than oceans.
According to GLAMOS, Swiss glaciers lost about a quarter of their volume between 2015 and 2025.
In 2025 alone, about 3 per cent was lost.

abschnitte.text: According to **MeteoSwiss**, Switzerland has become about **2.9 °C** warmer since **pre-industrial times** (as of 2025). Worldwide the warming is about **1.3 °C**. Switzerland is therefore warming about **twice as much**. One reason is that **land areas** warm more than oceans, and Switzerland lies far from the ocean.

The glacier monitoring network **GLAMOS** measures the Swiss glaciers every year. Between 2015 and 2025 their volume shrank by about **24 per cent**, that is, about **a quarter**. In 2025 alone about 3 per cent was lost. Small glaciers have already disappeared completely, and even large ones such as the **Aletsch Glacier** are getting shorter and shorter.

With the warming there are more **hot days** and less snow at low altitudes. Glaciers are important **water stores** for rivers and hydroelectric power stations. When they disappear, meltwater is missing in summer. In the mountains, soils thaw, which can make rockfalls more likely. The Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities are adapting to these changes.

gewusst: In just ten years the Swiss glaciers have lost about a quarter of their ice.
Some series of measurements by MeteoSwiss go back to the year 1864.

teile.einleitung: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a huge mountain range on the sea floor. It runs from north to south through the whole Atlantic. Here the Earth's plates drift apart, and new sea floor is constantly being formed.
wichtigste: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a mountain range under the sea.
It runs through the whole Atlantic.
The Earth's plates move apart there by a few centimetres a year.
Rising magma forms new sea floor.
Iceland and the Azores lie on the ridge.
In the 1950s Marie Tharp mapped the valley in its middle.

abschnitte.text: The **Mid-Atlantic Ridge** is a long chain of mountains on the **sea floor**. It reaches from the north near Iceland far into the south of the Atlantic. Most of its peaks lie deep under water. It is part of a worldwide network of **mid-ocean ridges** that run around the Earth like the seam of a tennis ball.

In the North Atlantic the ridge separates the **North American** and the **Eurasian Plate**. They move apart by about **2 to 5 centimetres** a year, roughly as fast as fingernails grow. In the gap **magma** rises, cools and forms new sea floor. That is why the sea floor is youngest right at the ridge. The further away, the older the rock.

In the 1950s the geologist **Marie Tharp**, with **Bruce Heezen**, drew maps of the sea floor. For this she used measurements of water depth taken by ships. She discovered a **rift valley** in the middle of the ridge. This was an important clue that the continents move.

In some places the ridge rises above the sea. The **Azores**, which belong to Portugal, are volcanic islands on the ridge. In **Iceland** the plate boundary even runs on land. In **Thingvellir** National Park you can see the rifts between the plates. South of Iceland, an eruption in the sea created the new island of **Surtsey** from 1963, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Off Brazil lie the small **Saint Peter and Saint Paul Rocks**. They consist of **peridotite**, a rock of the **Earth's mantle**. Normally such rock lies deep under the Earth's crust. Here it was lifted above sea level along a fracture zone.

gewusst: In Thingvellir you can dive in a rift between America and Europe.
On Surtsey only researchers are allowed ashore, so that people can observe how plants and animals settle a new island.

teile.einleitung: A monoculture is a field, a plantation or a forest on which only a single species of plant grows. This way of growing is practical and cheap, but it also causes big problems for soil and nature.
wichtigste: In a monoculture only one species of plant is grown on an area, often for many years.
Examples are oil palms, soya, maize, bananas or pure spruce forests.
Monocultures can be worked well with machines.
Pests and diseases spread easily in monocultures.
The soil can become depleted, and often a lot of pesticides are used.
Crop rotation and mixed cropping are ways to reduce the disadvantages.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek and Latin: “mono” means “alone” or “one”. In a **monoculture**, only a single crop grows over a large area. Well-known examples are huge **plantations** with oil palms in Indonesia and Malaysia, soya fields in Brazil or banana plantations in Central America. A forest in which only spruces stand is also a monoculture. The opposite is **mixed cropping**, in which different plants grow side by side.

Monocultures have advantages for farmers and companies. All the plants need the same care and are harvested at the same time. That is why big **machines** can be used and work is saved. Farmers can specialise in one plant and sell large quantities. In this way food and raw materials often become cheaper.

When the same plant grows everywhere, a **pest** finds a great deal of food and can spread quickly. Plant diseases, too, jump easily from plant to plant. That is why many farms use large amounts of **pesticides**. A well-known example from history is Ireland: around 1845 a disease destroyed the potatoes that very many people lived on. A severe famine followed.

If the same plant grows every year, it always takes the same nutrients from the soil. The soil becomes **depleted** and needs more fertiliser. In addition, in monocultures only a few animals and plants find a habitat, and **biodiversity** falls. For some plantations, large areas of rainforest were cleared. Pure spruce forests are also more vulnerable to storms and bark beetles.

An important method is **crop rotation**: on a field, different plants take turns from year to year, for example wheat, potatoes and clover. In Switzerland, farms that receive direct payments from the federal government must follow an orderly crop rotation. **Mixed cropping**, hedges and flower strips also help nature. In forests today, mixed stands of broadleaf and conifer trees are often planted.

gewusst: A large part of the world's palm oil comes from Indonesia and Malaysia.
Clover in a crop rotation improves the soil because, with the help of bacteria, it can fix nitrogen from the air.

teile.einleitung: Hummingbirds are tiny, colourful birds that live only in the Americas. They can stand still in the air and even fly backwards. They include the bee hummingbird, the smallest bird in the world.
wichtigste: Hummingbirds live wild only in North, Central and South America.
The bee hummingbird from Cuba, at about 5 to 6 centimetres, is the smallest bird in the world.
Hummingbirds drink nectar from flowers and eat small insects.
In hovering flight they stand still in the air, and they can fly backwards.
Small hummingbirds beat their wings many dozens of times a second.
At night they save energy in a state of torpor.

abschnitte.text: There are over 300 species of hummingbird. They live only in the **Americas**, most of them in **South America**. Many have an iridescent plumage in green, blue or red. The smallest is the **bee hummingbird** from Cuba. It is only about 5 to 6 centimetres long and weighs about 2 grams, about as much as a small coin. The biggest is the **giant hummingbird** from the Andes.

Hummingbirds drink sweet **nectar** from flowers. For this they have a long, thin **beak** and a long **tongue** that reaches deep into the flower. For protein they also eat small **insects**. When they drink, pollen sticks to them. In this way they carry it to the next flower and help the plants with **pollination**.

Hummingbirds are flying artists. They can fly forwards, sideways and even **backwards**. In **hovering flight** they move their wings so fast that they stand still in the air in front of a flower. Small hummingbirds beat their wings many dozens of times a second. That is why you can hardly see the wings. The fast beating makes a humming sound, which is why they are called **“hummingbirds”** in English, from “to hum”.

Flying fast takes a great deal of energy. Hummingbirds therefore have to keep drinking during the day. At night they cannot feed. Then they fall into a state of **torpor**. Their body cools down, and heart and breathing slow. In this way they need far less energy until the Sun rises in the morning.

Hummingbirds build small, cup-shaped **nests** from plant fibres, moss and spider webs. The spider webs make the nest stretchy. The females usually lay two tiny white eggs. The eggs of the bee hummingbird are hardly bigger than a pea.

gewusst: A hummingbird’s heart can beat over a thousand times a minute in flight.
Hummingbirds are the only birds that can really fly backwards.

teile.einleitung: The mistral is a cold, often stormy north wind in the south of France. It blows through the Rhône valley to the Mediterranean. In Provence it shapes the weather, the landscape and even the way houses are built.
wichtigste: The mistral is a cold north wind in the Rhône valley.
Between the Alps and the Massif Central it is accelerated as if in a funnel.
It often reaches storm force and can last several days.
It usually brings clear, dry and sunny weather.
In dry spells it increases the risk of forest fires.

abschnitte.text: The mistral arises when cold air flows from the north to the south towards the Mediterranean. Between the **Alps** and the **Massif Central**, the air is channelled through the narrow **Rhône valley**. As in a funnel, the wind gets faster. It often reaches **storm force** and can blow for days. Its name comes from the Occitan language and means something like “master wind”.

The mistral blows away clouds and haze. That is why in **Provence** it usually brings brilliant blue skies and very clear visibility. At the same time it is dry and cold, and even in summer it can feel cool. It dries out soil and plants, which in heat increases the risk of **forest fires**. Out over the sea, as far as Corsica and Sardinia, it can also make high waves.

The people of Provence have adapted to the mistral. Farmhouses often stand with their back to the north and have hardly any windows there. Rows of tall **cypresses** and hedges protect fields and gardens as **windbreaks**. Some trees grow crooked over time in the direction the wind blows.

gewusst: In Provence people say the mistral often lasts three, six or nine days.
Many painters came to Provence because of the clear light that the mistral brings with it.

teile.einleitung: In coral bleaching, corals lose their colour and turn white. It happens mainly when the sea water becomes too warm. If the heat lasts too long, the corals die.
wichtigste: Corals live together with tiny algae that give them colour and food.
When the water becomes too warm, the corals expel these algae.
Without the algae you can see the white limestone skeleton, and the coral bleaches.
If the heat lasts for a long time, the corals starve and die.
If the heat is only brief, corals can recover.
Because of global warming, coral bleaching is happening more and more often.

abschnitte.text: Reef corals are small animals that build a **limestone skeleton**. In their tissue live tiny **algae**, the **zooxanthellae**. These algae make sugar with sunlight and give part of it to the coral. In return they get a safe home. Both benefit from each other, which is called **symbiosis**. The algae also give the corals their beautiful colours.

If the sea water is too **warm** for a longer time, the partnership goes wrong. The corals expel their coloured algae. Now through the transparent tissue you can see the white **limestone skeleton**. The coral looks as if it had been bleached, hence the name **coral bleaching**. Just one to two degrees above the usual summer temperature can be enough over a few weeks.

A bleached coral is not yet dead. But it has hardly any food left. If the water cools down again soon, the algae can return, and the coral **recovers**. If the heat lasts too long, the coral **starves** and dies. Then other algae grow on the skeleton, and the reef loses its variety. Until a reef has recovered completely it often takes many years.

Because of **global warming** the oceans are getting warmer, and marine heatwaves are happening more often. That is why there are more and more big coral bleaching events. On the **Great Barrier Reef** in Australia, for example, huge areas bleached in 2016 and 2017. The sea also takes up a lot of **CO2** and becomes more acidic as a result. This makes it harder for corals to build their limestone skeleton.

gewusst: Some bleached corals briefly glow in bright colours before they turn white.
Coral reefs cover only a tiny part of the sea floor, but are home to a great many marine species.

teile.einleitung: Lavaux is a wine-growing area with steep vineyard terraces on the north shore of Lake Geneva in the canton of Vaud. The landscape is so special that it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Lavaux lies in the canton of Vaud on Lake Geneva.
It stretches for about 30 kilometres between Lausanne and the Vevey and Montreux area.
The first terraces were built in the Middle Ages under monasteries.
The most important grape variety is Chasselas.
Sun, lake and walls are the “three suns”.
Since 2007, Lavaux has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: **Lavaux** lies in the canton of **Vaud** on the north shore of **Lake Geneva**, which is called Lac Léman in French. The vineyards rise steeply from the shore. The area stretches for about 30 kilometres between **Lausanne** and the **Vevey** and **Montreux** area. So that vines can be grown on the steep slopes, countless **terraces** with stone walls were built. In between lie small winegrowing villages such as Cully, Lutry or Saint-Saphorin.

In the Middle Ages the area belonged to **monasteries** of the Benedictines and Cistercians. Under their rule, the first steep terraces were laid out from the **11th and 12th centuries**. For many centuries, winegrowing families have looked after and renewed the walls. That is how the landscape you see today came about. Since **2007**, Lavaux has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

It is said that the grapes in Lavaux are warmed by **three suns**. The first is the real **sun** in the sky. The second is the **lake**, which reflects the sunlight onto the slopes. The third is the **stone walls**, which store heat during the day and give it back in the evening. That is why the grapes ripen especially well here.

The most important grape variety in Lavaux is **Chasselas**, called **Gutedel** in German. It is the typical white wine grape of western Switzerland. A well-known vineyard is the **Dézaley** between Lutry and Saint-Saphorin. Its wines carry the label **Grand Cru**, which is an award for especially good sites. Many visitors walk along paths through the vines and enjoy the view across the lake to the Alps.

gewusst: Small tourist trains run through the vineyards of Lavaux, so you can explore the terraces comfortably.
In Vevey, the big winegrowers' festival, the Fête des Vignerons, takes place about every 20 to 25 years.

teile.einleitung: Lake-effect snow is a weather phenomenon on big lakes in which a great deal of snow can fall in a short time. It is especially well known on the Great Lakes in North America.
wichtigste: “Lake effect” means that the lake itself causes the effect (in German it is called “Seeeffekt”).
Cold air moves across a lake that is still warmer and not frozen.
The air picks up warmth and moisture on the way.
On the downwind shore it snows in strong bands.
The city of Buffalo on Lake Erie, for example, is known for this.

abschnitte.text: In late autumn and early winter, the water of the **Great Lakes** is still warmer than the air. When icy **polar air** then flows over the lake, it picks up **warmth** and **moisture** from below. The moist air rises and cools. Dense clouds form. When they reach the shore, it snows heavily.

abschnitte.titel: Snow bands on the lee shore
abschnitte.text: The snow falls mainly on the **lee shore**, that is, the side that the wind blows towards. On the Great Lakes this is usually the east or south shore. The snow often comes in narrow **bands**. In one place a lot of snow then falls, while a few kilometres away it hardly snows at all. Well known for this are the city of **Buffalo** on Lake Erie and areas east of Lake Ontario.

The effect works only as long as the lake is not frozen over. If it freezes, the moisture is missing and the lake effect stops. Something similar also happens over seas, for example on the west coast of Japan, where cold winds blow across the Sea of Japan. There, too, a great deal of snow falls in some mountains.

gewusst: In November 2014, more than a metre of snow fell in the Buffalo area within a few days.

teile.einleitung: The Congo is a huge river in Central Africa. It is the river with the most water in Africa and the deepest river in the world. It flows in a great arc through the rainforest and empties into the Atlantic.
wichtigste: After the Nile, the Congo is the second longest river in Africa, about 4,400 to 4,700 kilometres long depending on how it is measured.
It carries more water than any other river in Africa.
In some places it is over 200 metres deep, and no river is deeper.
The Congo crosses the Equator twice.
The capital cities Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across the river.
It empties into the Atlantic on the west coast of Africa.

abschnitte.text: Depending on how it is measured, the Congo is about 4,400 to 4,700 kilometres long. Only the **Nile** is longer in Africa. But the Congo carries the most water, much more than the Nile. In the world only the **Amazon** has more water. In some places the Congo is over **200 metres deep**. That makes it the **deepest river** in the world.

The Congo flows in a great **arc** through Central Africa. First it flows north, then west and finally south-west. In doing so it crosses the **Equator** twice. Because its basin lies north and south of the Equator, it is always raining somewhere. That is why it carries a lot of water all year round. On the west coast of Africa it empties into the **Atlantic Ocean**.

A large part of the river flows through the **rainforest**, the second biggest on Earth. There it rains a great deal. Many tributaries join the Congo. For people the river is an important **transport route**, because there are only a few roads in the dense forest. On the Congo, boats and barges carry people and goods.

On the Congo there are many **rapids** and waterfalls. At the city of **Kisangani** lie the **Boyoma Falls**. They consist of several steps over about 100 kilometres and used to be called the **Stanley Falls**. Between Kinshasa and the sea too, the river plunges over many rapids. That is why ships cannot sail from the sea deep into the country.

Two countries bear the name of the river: the **Democratic Republic of the Congo** and the **Republic of the Congo**. Their capital cities **Kinshasa** and **Brazzaville** face each other directly across the river. Only the Congo separates them. The broad river is also a border for animals. **Bonobos** live only south of it, because they cannot swim.

gewusst: Apart from Rome and Vatican City, no two capital cities in the world lie as close together as Kinshasa and Brazzaville.
In the deep Congo live species of fish that occur nowhere else.

teile.einleitung: Magma is molten rock deep inside the Earth. When it reaches the surface in a volcanic eruption, it is called lava.
wichtigste: Magma is hot, liquid rock beneath the Earth's surface.
It mostly comes from the mantle beneath the Earth's crust.
Because it is lighter than the rock around it, it rises.
Gases are dissolved in magma, for example water vapour.
At the surface, the molten rock is called lava.
When magma cools slowly deep down, granite, for example, forms.

abschnitte.text: **Magma** is molten rock. It is very hot and therefore liquid, roughly like thick porridge. The word comes from Greek and means “kneaded mass”. Magma forms mainly in the **mantle**, the layer beneath the Earth's crust. It is so hot there that rock can melt.

Hot magma is lighter than the solid rock around it. That is why it slowly rises, rather like an air bubble in water. Beneath many volcanoes it collects in a **magma chamber** a few kilometres down. **Gases** are also dissolved in magma, such as water vapour, just as carbon dioxide is in a bottle of fizzy water.

If too much magma and gas collect beneath a volcano, the pressure keeps growing. At some point the volcano erupts. As soon as the molten rock comes out at the surface, it is called **lava**. Beforehand, researchers often notice that the ground rises slightly and trembles. Instruments show this, so people can be warned in time.

When magma cools, it becomes solid and new rock forms. If it cools very slowly deep in the Earth, large crystals form. This is how **granite**, with its clearly visible grains, is formed. Granite is also found in the **Swiss Alps**, for example in the Gotthard area. If lava solidifies quickly at the surface, the rock becomes fine-grained, as with **basalt**.

gewusst: Granite is solidified magma that never reached the Earth's surface but became visible only through erosion.
Magma and lava are the same material, and only the place decides the name.

teile.einleitung: A lagoon is a shallow body of water on the coast that is separated from the open sea by sandbanks, islands or reefs. Lagoons are important habitats, and some cities have even been built in the middle of a lagoon.
wichtigste: A lagoon is a shallow coastal body of water, largely cut off from the sea.
It is connected to the sea through narrow openings.
The word comes from the Latin “lacuna”, meaning a hollow or pond.
Venice lies in a lagoon that is separated from the Adriatic by the Lido.
The salt content depends greatly on rivers and evaporation.
Lagoons are a sheltered nursery for young fish.

abschnitte.text: A **lagoon** is a shallow body of water on the coast. Long strips of sand, known as **spits**, islands or **reefs** separate it largely from the open sea. Seawater flows in and out only through narrow openings. The word comes via the Italian “laguna” from the Latin **“lacuna”**. That means a hollow, a gap or a pond.

Long, narrow sand islands off a coast are called **barrier islands**. Between them and the mainland there are often shallow lagoons. A well-known example is the **Outer Banks** in the USA. In Spain, the narrow spit of La Manga separates the **Mar Menor** from the Mediterranean. It is one of the biggest saltwater lagoons in Europe. In tropical **atolls**, too, there is a lagoon in the middle, surrounded by a coral reef.

The city of **Venice** was built on islands in the middle of a lagoon. The long sand island of the **Lido** separates the lagoon from the Adriatic. The Venice Film Festival takes place there every year. In storm surges, Venice is in danger of being flooded. That is why the **MOSE** system was built: flap gates on the sea floor rise up when the water is high. In 2020 it was used successfully against a storm surge for the first time.

Because the exchange with the sea is limited, the **salt content** changes a great deal. Where rivers bring a lot of **fresh water**, the water is **brackish**, that is, only slightly salty. Where it is hot and a lot of water **evaporates**, a lagoon can even become saltier than the sea. The animals and plants have to cope with these differences.

The water in lagoons is calm, shallow and **rich in nutrients**. It gives shelter from big waves and from predators from the open sea. That is why many **young fish** and crabs spend their youth in lagoons. Many waterbirds also find food here. Lagoons are therefore often protected nature areas.

gewusst: In Venice, people get around not by car but by boat and on foot.
The Lido of Venice is about eleven kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: The Lena is one of the great rivers of Siberia in Russia. It flows north into the Arctic Ocean and is frozen for many months of the year.
wichtigste: The Lena rises in a mountain range near Lake Baikal.
It flows mainly northwards.
It enters the Laptev Sea, a marginal sea of the Arctic Ocean, through a huge delta.
The city of Yakutsk lies on the bank of the Lena on permafrost ground.
The Lena Pillars have been a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site since 2012.
In the long winter the river is frozen.

abschnitte.text: The Lena rises in a mountain range west of **Lake Baikal**. From there it flows in a great curve and then mainly **northwards** through eastern Siberia. At about 4,400 kilometres, it is one of the longest rivers on Earth. It enters the **Laptev Sea**, part of the **Arctic Ocean**.

The biggest city on the river is **Yakutsk**, the capital of the Republic of **Sakha**, also called Yakutia. There the ground is deeply frozen all year round, which is called **permafrost**. So that the warmth of the houses does not thaw the ground, many buildings stand on **stilts**. Yakutsk is regarded as one of the coldest big cities in the world.

On the bank of the Lena, the **Lena Pillars** rise for many kilometres. These are towers of **limestone** rock up to 100 metres high. Wind, frost and water have shaped them over a long time. Since **2012** they have been a **UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site**.

At its mouth, the Lena splits into many channels and forms a huge **delta** with countless islands. It is one of the biggest river deltas on Earth. In the short Arctic summer, a great many birds breed there. A large part of the delta is therefore a **protected area**.

In the long Siberian winter the Lena freezes over. Then it is hardly navigable for ships. The thick ice is even partly used as a **road** for lorries. When the ice breaks in spring, ice jams and **floods** can occur.

gewusst: In Yakutsk it can get colder than minus 40 degrees in winter.
The Lena flows almost entirely through areas with permafrost.

teile.einleitung: Mauna Loa is a huge volcano on the island of Hawaii in the Pacific. It is one of the biggest volcanoes on Earth and is still active today.
wichtigste: Mauna Loa lies on the island of Hawaii, also called the Big Island.
It covers about half of the island.
“Mauna Loa” means “long mountain” in Hawaiian.
The summit lies about 4,170 metres above sea level.
It last erupted at the end of 2022, after 38 years of quiet.
Since 1958, the carbon dioxide content of the air has been measured there.

abschnitte.text: **Mauna Loa** stands on the island of **Hawaii**, which is also called the **Big Island**. The island consists of five volcanoes, and Mauna Loa covers about 51 per cent of its area. Its name means “long mountain” in Hawaiian: “mauna” means mountain, and “loa” means long. This suits its wide, gentle slopes. Such flat volcanoes are called **shield volcanoes**.

The summit lies about **4,169 metres** above sea level. But the volcano begins deep under water on the sea floor. Measured from there, it is much higher. Its neighbour, **Mauna Kea**, is a little higher at about 4,207 metres. Measured from the sea floor, Mauna Kea is even more than 10,000 metres high.

Mauna Loa is an **active volcano**. At the end of **November 2022**, an eruption began that lasted about two weeks. Before that the volcano had been quiet for 38 years. Its lava is rather runny and flows down the slopes in long streams.

abschnitte.titel: A measuring station for the climate
abschnitte.text: At the **Mauna Loa Observatory**, the content of **carbon dioxide** in the air has been measured since **1958**. The place is well suited because it lies far from big cities and factories. The curve of the measurements is called the **Keeling Curve**, after the researcher Charles David Keeling. It shows that the content of this greenhouse gas is rising steadily.

gewusst: Mauna Loa alone covers about half of Hawaii's biggest island.
The Keeling Curve from Mauna Loa is one of the best-known series of measurements in climate research.

teile.einleitung: The climate classification by Köppen and Geiger divides the Earth into climate zones. Each zone is given letters that show how warm and how wet it is there.
wichtigste: Wladimir Köppen developed the climate classification around 1900.
Rudolf Geiger later extended it.
There are five main groups with the letters A to E.
A stands for tropical climates, B for dry climates.
The basis is temperature and precipitation.

abschnitte.text: The climate researcher **Wladimir Köppen** developed around 1900 a division of the world’s climates. In doing so he also took his lead from the **plant world**, because plants show well what climate prevails at a place. Later the researcher **Rudolf Geiger** revised and extended the division. That is why today people speak of the classification by **Köppen and Geiger**.

Each climate zone is given a capital letter. **A** stands for the **tropical climates**, where it is warm all year. **B** denotes the **dry climates** such as deserts and steppes, where more water evaporates than falls as precipitation. **C** are the warm temperate climates, **D** the cold climates with snowy winters. **E** stands for the **polar climates** with ice and tundra.

After the first letter, more often follow. They say, for example, whether it rains all year or whether one season is dry, and how warm the summer gets. Large parts of the **Swiss Central Plateau** have the climate **Cfb**: warm temperate, humid all year, with warm summers. In the high Alps, by contrast, much colder climates prevail. In this way places all over the world can be compared with a short code.

gewusst: The Köppen-Geiger classification is still used today in school books and in research all over the world.
With climate change the boundaries of the climate zones are slowly shifting.

teile.einleitung: The Llano Estacado is a huge, very flat plateau in the south of the Great Plains in the USA. It lies in the states of Texas and New Mexico and is one of the flattest large landscapes in North America.
wichtigste: The Llano Estacado lies in the south of the Great Plains in Texas and New Mexico.
It is one of the flattest large areas in North America.
Steep escarpments, the “Caprock Escarpments”, bound the plateau.
The name comes from Spanish.
Today a lot of farming is carried on there using groundwater.

abschnitte.text: The **Llano Estacado** is a **plateau**: the land lies high but is almost completely flat. You can drive for long distances there without seeing a hill. On three sides the plain is bounded by steep escarpments, the **Caprock Escarpments**. A hard layer of rock on top protects the plain from erosion, which is why it has stayed so level.

The name is **Spanish**. “Llano” means plain, but exactly how “Estacado” is meant is not entirely certain. Spanish explorers crossed the area as early as the 16th century. For a long time the plain was the territory of the **Comanche**, who hunted bison there. Later came cattle ranchers and farmers.

It does not rain very much, and there are hardly any rivers. Even so, a lot is grown there, above all **cotton**. The water for it comes from a huge underground store, the **Ogallala Aquifer**. Because more water is pumped out than flows back in, the water table is falling. Well-known cities on or at the edge of the plain are **Lubbock** and **Amarillo**.

gewusst: On the Llano Estacado there are thousands of small, shallow hollows that fill with water after rain.
The Ogallala Aquifer extends beneath several US states.

teile.einleitung: The Latin American city is a model that geographers use to describe the typical layout of big cities in Central and South America. It shows how colonial times, rural depopulation and great differences between rich and poor have shaped these cities.
wichtigste: At the centre of the Spanish colonial city lies the Plaza Mayor.
In 1573, royal regulations, later part of the Leyes de Indias, fixed the layout.
In colonial times, social status fell from the centre outwards.
Bahr and Mertins developed a well-known city model in 1981.
Because of rural depopulation, the cities grew very quickly in the 20th century.
Informal settlements are called favelas, villas miseria or pueblos jóvenes, depending on the country.

abschnitte.text: The Spanish founded many cities in the Americas according to a fixed plan. King **Philip II** issued regulations for this in 1573, which became part of the **Leyes de Indias**. They demanded a central square and a **right-angled street grid** that looks like a chessboard. Around the main square, the **Plaza Mayor**, stood the cathedral, the town hall and the governor's seat. In Mexico the main square is often called the **Zócalo**.

In colonial times the **upper class** lived right on the plaza, close to the church and to power. The further from the centre, the **poorer** the residents were. This is the opposite of many North American cities, where wealthy families tend to live on the edge of the city. Later, in Latin America too, many rich people moved away from the old centre to new districts.

The German geographers **Jürgen Bahr** and **Günter Mertins** developed a well-known model in 1981. They described the city as having **ring-shaped**, **sector-shaped** and **cell-shaped** parts. Their model is often used in geography lessons in German-speaking countries. As early as 1980, **Griffin and Ford** had presented a model. In it there is the **spine**, an axis running out from the centre, along which the shops and upper-class residential districts lie.

In the 20th century, very many people moved from the countryside to the cities in search of work. This **rural depopulation** made cities such as Mexico City, São Paulo or Lima grow very quickly. There were too few homes for the many newcomers. That is why **informal settlements** sprang up on open land on the **edge of the city** and on **steep slopes**, which were not much in demand and often had no services.

abschnitte.titel: Rich and poor side by side
abschnitte.text: The informal settlements have their own names, depending on the country. In Brazil they are called **favelas**, in Argentina **villas miseria** and in Peru **pueblos jóvenes**, which means “young villages”. In cities such as **Rio de Janeiro**, favelas on hillsides often lie right next to rich districts. Rich and poor are close to each other in space but sharply divided socially. This division is called **segregation**.

gewusst: Many informal settlements have been built up over time and today have solid houses, electricity and water.
The Zócalo in Mexico City is one of the biggest squares in the world.

teile.einleitung: The lion is a big cat and is often called the “king of the beasts”. It is the only cat that lives in large groups, known as prides.
wichtigste: Almost all wild lions live in Africa south of the Sahara.
Adult male lions have a big mane.
Lions mostly live in the savanna.
In a pride, it is mostly the lionesses that hunt together.
Lions hunt big animals such as zebras, wildebeest and antelopes.
In the Gir Forest in India, a small group of Asiatic lions still lives.

abschnitte.text: Because of its strength and its splendid **mane**, the lion is often called the **“king of the beasts”**. Only the adult males have a mane around the head and neck, the **lionesses** do not. After the tiger, lions are the biggest cats in the world. Their roar can be heard for kilometres.

Lions live mainly in the **savanna**. This is open grassland with scattered trees. Almost all wild lions live in **Africa** south of the Sahara. Lions rest a great deal, and often sleep or doze for most of the day. They are mainly active at dusk and at night.

Lions live in **prides**. A pride usually consists of several related lionesses, their cubs and one or a few males. The males mainly protect the **territory** and drive away strange lions. The lionesses raise the cubs together.

Lions are **meat eaters**. Mostly the **lionesses** hunt together. They creep up and surround their prey. This way they can also catch big animals such as **zebras**, **wildebeest** and **antelopes**. Lions are not long-distance runners, so they have to get close to their prey.

In the past, lions also lived in southern Europe, the Middle East and large parts of Asia. Today in Asia there is only a small group of **Asiatic lions** in the **Gir Forest** in the west of **India**. There they are strictly protected. In Africa, too, the number of lions has fallen sharply in recent decades.

gewusst: The lion is the only species of cat that lives in large groups.
A lion can rest for up to 20 hours a day.

teile.einleitung: Every good map has a legend. It explains what the signs and colours on the map mean. If you can read the legend, you understand any map much better.
wichtigste: The legend is the explanation of the signs on a map.
That is why it is also called the key.
The legend is usually at the edge or in a corner of the map.
If you do not know a sign, you look it up in the legend.
Every map has its own legend, because maps use different signs.
Only signs and colours belong in the legend, not the weather.

abschnitte.text: On a map everything is much smaller than in reality. That is why houses, paths and lakes are drawn with simple signs. The **legend** explains every sign and every colour. Without a legend a map is **hard** to read, because you would have to guess. That is why every good map has one.

The legend is usually **at the edge** of the map or in a corner. This way it does not cover anything important. On folding maps it is often on the back or in a separate box. If you do not know a sign, you look for it in the legend and read next to it what it means.

On a **hiking map**, the legend shows how hiking trails, huts and mountain railways are drawn. If the legend says “lake” next to a blue box, then every blue area on this map is a lake. On a **height map**, a height in metres is given next to each colour. This way you know how high the land is at any point.

Not all maps use the same signs and colours. A city map needs different signs from a hiking map or a world map. That is why every map explains its own signs. Only things that are drawn on the map belong in the legend, for example not the **weather forecast**.

gewusst: Plans of school buildings or zoos often have a small legend too.
On maps in Switzerland, the legend often also shows PostBus stops and mountain railways.

teile.einleitung: Kiwis are special birds from New Zealand. They cannot fly, are out and about at night and have their nostrils at the tip of the beak. The kiwi is so popular that the people of New Zealand call themselves “Kiwis”.
wichtigste: Kiwis live only in New Zealand.
They cannot fly and have only tiny wings.
Kiwis are nocturnal.
Their nostrils lie right at the tip of the beak.
They eat mainly worms and insects.
A kiwi is about as big as a domestic hen.

abschnitte.text: The **kiwi** has only tiny wings that you can hardly see under the feathers. It can never fly. It runs over the ground on short, strong legs. A kiwi is about as big as a **domestic hen** and has a round body. Its **feathers** are thin and soft and look more like a fur of hairs.

Kiwis are **nocturnal**. By day they sleep in caves, hollow tree trunks or under dense plants. Their plumage is mostly **brownish** to greyish brown. In this way they are well camouflaged on the forest floor. In the dark they rely mainly on hearing, touch and smell.

The kiwi is the only bird with **nostrils at the tip of the beak**. With its long beak it probes the ground. In this way it smells **worms**, beetles and larvae hidden underground. Insects and sometimes fruit are also part of its food.

The kiwi’s **egg** is huge compared with its body. It weighs about a fifth as much as the female. Hardly any other bird lays such a big egg in proportion to its own size. Many kinds of kiwi are **endangered** today, because introduced animals such as stoats and cats hunt the young birds.

The kiwi is the best-known animal of **New Zealand**. New Zealanders often call themselves **“Kiwis”**. The kiwi fruit too was named after the bird, because it also looks brown and hairy. In New Zealand there are many projects to protect the birds.

gewusst: The kiwi is the only bird in the world with nostrils at the tip of its beak.
In proportion to the bird, a kiwi egg is one of the biggest eggs of all birds.

teile.einleitung: Continentality describes how strongly the climate of a place is shaped by the land rather than by the sea. In the interior of large continents the summers are hot and the winters very cold. On the coasts the sea evens out the temperatures.
wichtigste: Water stores a lot of heat and warms up more slowly than land.
That is why the annual range, the difference between the warmest and the coldest month, is small on coasts.
The maritime climate has cool summers, mild winters and high humidity.
In the continental climate the summers are hot, the winters cold and the daily swings large.
Yakutsk in eastern Siberia has an extremely continental climate.
In Europe continentality increases from west to east.
Switzerland lies in the transition between maritime and continental climate.

abschnitte.titel: Why the sea evens things out
abschnitte.text: Water has a high **heat capacity**. It takes a lot of energy to warm up, and gives the heat back only slowly. In addition, the heat is spread into the depths by mixing. Land, by contrast, heats up quickly and cools quickly. That is why on coasts the sea dampens summer heat and winter cold. The difference between the warmest and the coldest month is called the **annual range**. It is small on coasts and large in the interior of continents.

In the **maritime climate** the summers are **cool** and the winters **mild**. The air is humid, there are many clouds and frequent precipitation. One example is Ireland. Because the sea warms only slowly, in many coastal places it is not July but **August** that is the warmest month. This delay is passed from the water to the air.

In the **continental climate** the summers are hot and the winters very cold. An extreme example is **Yakutsk** in eastern Siberia. There the monthly means in winter are around minus 40 degrees, and the summers are warm. Its annual range is among the biggest of all the cities in the world. Temperatures also swing strongly over the course of a day. Dry air and few clouds let the ground become hot by day and cool strongly at night.

In the middle latitudes the **westerlies** mostly blow. They bring moist, balanced sea air from the Atlantic to Europe. The further east you go, the weaker this influence becomes. If you travel from Ireland to the Urals, the winters get colder and the summers warmer. For the same reason **west coasts** usually have a more maritime climate than **east coasts** at the same latitude. On east coasts the air often comes from the continent. With a **continentality index**, for example the one by Gorczyński, continentality can be given as a number.

Switzerland lies in a **transition zone**. It receives Atlantic sea air from the west, but is also exposed to continental influences from the east. In addition, the **Alps** shape the climate strongly. The **Valais** is drier and more continental than the Central Plateau. It lies in the **rain shadow** of the Bernese and Valais Alps, which let the moist air rain out beforehand.

gewusst: The central Valais is among the driest areas in Switzerland.
In Yakutsk the difference between the coldest and the warmest month can be almost 60 degrees.

teile.einleitung: The Mediterranean is a big sea between Europe, Africa and Asia. It is almost entirely enclosed by land and connected to other seas only by narrow passages. For thousands of years it has been an important link for trade, travel and cultures, and today it is a popular holiday destination.
wichtigste: The Mediterranean borders three continents: Europe, Africa and Asia.
The Strait of Gibraltar connects the Mediterranean with the Atlantic.
The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean with the Red Sea.
Sicily is the biggest island in the Mediterranean.
There are hardly any tides in the Mediterranean.
The Mediterranean is saltier than the Atlantic because a lot of water evaporates.
Around the Mediterranean, ancient civilisations such as Egypt, Greece and Rome arose.

abschnitte.text: The Mediterranean covers about 2.5 million square kilometres, roughly sixty times the size of Switzerland. In the north lie countries such as Spain, France, Italy, Greece and Turkey, in the south Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco. In the east it borders Asia, with countries such as Israel, Lebanon and Syria. Parts of the Mediterranean have names of their own, for example the **Adriatic** or the Aegean.

In the west the **Strait of Gibraltar**, between Spain and Morocco, leads into the Atlantic, and at its narrowest point it is only about 14 kilometres wide. In the south-east the **Suez Canal** in Egypt connects the Mediterranean with the Red Sea and so with the Indian Ocean. It opened in 1869 and saves ships the long way round Africa. In the north-east the Dardanelles and the Bosporus lead into the Black Sea.

In the Mediterranean lie thousands of islands. The biggest is **Sicily**, which belongs to Italy and is home to the volcano Etna. Other big islands are Sardinia, Cyprus, Corsica and Crete. The Balearic Islands with Majorca are well-known holiday islands too.

On the Mediterranean some of the oldest **civilisations** arose, for example in Egypt, Greece and Phoenicia. The Romans later ruled all its coasts and called it “mare nostrum”, our sea. Over the Mediterranean, goods such as olive oil, wine and grain were traded, but knowledge, religions and writing were also spread. About six million years ago it was at times almost dried out, because the connection to the Atlantic was closed.

Around the Mediterranean the **Mediterranean climate** prevails, with hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters. Typical plants are olive trees, cypresses, pines and citrus fruits. In the sea there are seagrass meadows, and dolphins, tuna and sea turtles live there. Problems are overfishing, pollution and the warming of the water.

Every year millions of people, many of them from Switzerland, spend their holidays on the Mediterranean. Tourism is an important source of income for many coastal countries. At the same time the Mediterranean is, for many people from Africa and Asia, a dangerous **escape route** to Europe. Many people have already lost their lives on crossings in small, overcrowded boats.

begriffe.erklaerung: A narrow place where two seas are connected.
A waterway for ships built by people.
A climate with hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters.
An early society with cities, writing and great buildings.

gewusst: The name Mediterranean means “sea in the middle of the lands”.
Because there are hardly any tides, the beach on the Mediterranean stays about the same width all day.
From Switzerland, the Rhône flows through Lake Geneva all the way to the Mediterranean.

teile.einleitung: The scale shows how much a map has been reduced. With it you can convert distances on the map into real distances and the other way round.
wichtigste: The scale gives the reduction ratio of a map.
At 1:25,000, 1 cm on the map corresponds to 25,000 cm in reality.
At 1:100,000, 1 cm stands for exactly 1 km.
The smaller the scale number, the larger the scale.
With the scale bar you can measure distances directly.
To convert, you multiply or divide by the scale number.

abschnitte.text: A map shows reality greatly reduced. The **scale** says how much. At **1:25,000**, 1 cm on the map corresponds to 25,000 cm in reality. So everything in reality is 25,000 times bigger than on the map. The Swiss **national maps** come, for example, in scales of 1:25,000 and 1:50,000.

If you want to know a real distance, you **multiply** the distance on the map by the scale number. Example: 6 cm on a 1:25,000 map gives 6 times 25,000 equals 150,000 cm. That is 1,500 m or **1.5 km**. On a 1:200,000 map, 5 cm already gives 1,000,000 cm, that is **10 km**. At the end it is important to convert the units: 100 cm make 1 m, and 100,000 cm make 1 km.

The other way round, you **divide** the real distance by the scale number. Two places are 3 km apart, which is 300,000 cm. On a 1:50,000 map, that is 300,000 divided by 50,000, so **6 cm**. You can also work out the scale itself: if 4 cm correspond to exactly 1 km, you calculate 100,000 divided by 4. That gives **1:25,000**.

The smaller the number after the colon, the **larger** the scale. A 1:10,000 map therefore has a larger scale than a 1:100,000 map. It shows a small area with many **details**. A map with a small scale, on the other hand, shows a large area, such as a whole country.

At the edge of many maps a **scale bar** is drawn. It shows distances as a line with figures in metres or kilometres. With a ruler or a piece of string you can measure a distance on the map and compare it directly with the bar. This is handy because you do not have to calculate. For winding routes such as hiking trails, a piece of string works especially well.

gewusst: At 1:25,000, 4 cm on the map correspond to exactly 1 km in reality.
A “large” scale number means a small scale, and many people mix this up.

teile.einleitung: Climatology is the science of climate. It examines how the atmosphere behaves over a long time. To do so it analyses series of measurements covering many decades.
wichtigste: Climatology is the science that studies climate.
It examines the long-term behaviour of the atmosphere.
It analyses series of measurements over many decades.
Meteorology, by contrast, studies mainly the weather.

abschnitte.text: **Climatology** studies the **climate**, that is, the weather over many years. Climatologists analyse long **series of measurements** of temperature, precipitation, wind and sunshine. They compare places and periods with one another. From this they recognise how the climate is made up and how it changes.

**Meteorology** deals mainly with the **weather** and makes, for example, weather forecasts. Climatology looks at **long periods**. The two subjects are closely related and often use the same measurements. In Switzerland the federal office **MeteoSwiss** collects such data, and some series of measurements go back to the 19th century.

For the time before measuring instruments, people use **traces in nature**. These include ice cores from glaciers, tree rings or deposits in lakes. In this way the climate of past millennia can be studied. These results also help to understand today’s **climate change** better.

gewusst: Air bubbles in the ice of Antarctica reveal what the air was made up of hundreds of thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: Coke is a grey, hard and porous fuel made from hard coal. It is especially important for obtaining iron from iron ore in the blast furnace. Without coke there would hardly be any steel.
wichtigste: Coke forms when hard coal is heated strongly with the air shut out.
In the process gases and tar escape, and almost pure carbon is left behind.
The plant in which coke is made is called a coking plant.
In the blast furnace, coke supplies the heat and helps to obtain iron from iron ore.
Coke is lighter and more porous than coal and burns very hot.

abschnitte.text: In a **coking plant**, **hard coal** is heated strongly in large ovens without any air getting in. This process is called **coking**. The coal cannot burn in the process. Instead, gases, water and **tar** escape. What is left is a grey, holey substance that consists almost entirely of **carbon**. That is coke.

Coke is needed above all for making **iron** and **steel**. In the **blast furnace**, iron ore and coke are stacked in layers. The coke burns and supplies very great **heat**. At the same time it removes the **oxygen** from the iron ore. In this way liquid **pig iron** is produced, from which steel is later made. Because coke is hard and porous, it bears the heavy load in the furnace and still lets air through.

In the past, **charcoal** was needed to smelt iron. For this, whole forests were cut down. In the 18th century people in England began to smelt iron with coke made from hard coal. This was an important step in **industrialisation**. Soon many coking plants and steelworks sprang up in coal regions such as the Ruhr.

When coal is coked, **coke oven gas** and tar are produced. The gas was once used as town gas for cooking and for street lamps. From tar, substances for paints and medicines were obtained. The production and use of coke, however, releases a lot of **CO2**. That is why the steel industry is looking for new processes, for example with **hydrogen** instead of coke.

gewusst: Coke is so porous that it feels much lighter than an equally big piece of coal.
In the past, stoves in many Swiss homes were heated with coke.

teile.einleitung: The Maghreb is a region in north-west Africa between the Mediterranean, the Atlantic and the Sahara. The name comes from Arabic and means “west” or “the place where the sun sets”.
wichtigste: In Arabic, Maghreb means “west” or “place of the sunset”.
The core is made up of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia.
In a wider sense, Libya and Mauritania are also counted.
On the coast there is a Mediterranean climate with rain in winter.
In 1989, five states founded the Arab Maghreb Union in Marrakesh.
The status of Western Sahara is still disputed today.

abschnitte.text: Seen from the Arabian Peninsula, north-west Africa lies to the west, hence the name **Maghreb**. In the narrower sense it includes **Morocco**, **Algeria** and **Tunisia**. In a wider sense, **Libya** and **Mauritania** are also counted as part of the Maghreb. In the north the region borders the Mediterranean, in the west the Atlantic and in the south the Sahara.

On the coast the climate is Mediterranean: summers are hot and dry, and rain falls mainly in winter. That is why **olives**, **citrus fruits** and grapes grow there. The **Atlas** mountains run through the region. Further south it becomes drier and drier until the desert begins. Dry valleys that carry water only after heavy rain are called **oueds**, from the Arabic word “wadi”.

In dry areas water is precious. In Morocco, **khettaras** carry groundwater to the oases. These are gently sloping underground channels with vertical shafts. The water flows from the edge of the mountains to the fields without any pumps. In Iran the same system is known as a **qanat**.

People of Arab and **Amazigh** origin live in the Maghreb, and the Amazigh used to be called Berbers. Many people speak Arabic, many also speak an Amazigh language, and French is often used. A centre of Amazigh culture is **Kabylia**, a mountain region east of Algiers in the Tell Atlas. Its inhabitants, the Kabyles, have a language of their own.

In 1989, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Mauritania founded the **Arab Maghreb Union** in Marrakesh. They wanted to cooperate more closely in economic matters. Because of political tensions, however, the Union is largely blocked. One point of dispute is **Western Sahara** on the Atlantic coast: Morocco claims the territory, while the **Polisario** movement demands a state of its own. The UN lists it as a non-self-governing territory.

gewusst: After a thunderstorm, an oued can turn into a raging torrent in a short time.
The khettaras have worked for centuries entirely without motors, using only the slope of the ground.

teile.einleitung: Colombia is a country in the north-west of South America. It is known for coffee, emeralds and a huge variety of animals and plants. It is the only country in South America that lies on both the Pacific and the Caribbean Sea.
wichtigste: The capital city of Colombia is Bogotá, which lies at a height of about 2,600 metres.
Colombia borders the Pacific and the Caribbean Sea.
The country is named after the navigator Christopher Columbus.
Colombia has more species of birds than any other country in the world.
It is famous for coffee, emeralds and cut flowers.
Panama belonged to Colombia until 1903.
The national language is Spanish.

abschnitte.text: Colombia has a coast on the **Pacific** in the west and on the **Caribbean Sea** in the north. Through the country run the **Andes**, which divide here into three mountain ranges. Between them flows the great river **Magdalena**. In the south-east lies part of the **Amazon rainforest**. The capital city **Bogotá** lies high in the mountains at about 2,600 metres and is the biggest city in the country.

Colombia is named after **Christopher Columbus**, who came to America in 1492. Later the **Spanish** conquered the area. On the Caribbean coast they founded the port city of **Cartagena** and protected it with a thick wall. Its old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site today. At the beginning of the 19th century the country became independent under the leadership of **Simón Bolívar**. **Panama** belonged to Colombia until 1903 and then separated with the support of the USA.

Colombia is one of the countries with the most species of animals and plants in the world. Almost **2,000 species of birds** live here, more than in any other country. In addition there are monkeys, jaguars, sloths and countless frogs and butterflies. The reason is the great variety of landscapes: coasts, rainforest, high mountains and grassland lie close together.

Colombia is one of the biggest **coffee producers** in the world. The **coffee-growing landscape** in the mountains is even a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The country is also famous for **emeralds**, bright green gemstones. Many of the finest emeralds in the world come from here. In greenhouses on the high plateau around Bogotá, **roses** and **carnations** grow. In **cut flowers**, Colombia is, after the Netherlands, the second biggest exporter in the world.

The **flag** has a broad **yellow** stripe at the top, with a blue one and a red one beneath it. The writer **Gabriel García Márquez** from Colombia received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982. For decades the country suffered from an armed conflict. In 2016 the government concluded a peace agreement with the biggest rebel group, the **FARC**.

gewusst: The flag of Colombia is yellow, blue and red, with yellow taking up the whole upper half.
The national bird of Colombia is the Andean condor, one of the biggest flying birds in the world.

teile.einleitung: The coconut palm is a tall palm that grows on warm beaches in the tropics. Its fruit is the coconut. From the palm people make food, drinks, oil, ropes and even doormats.
wichtigste: The fruit of the coconut palm is called a coconut.
A coconut palm can grow up to about 30 metres tall.
The coconut is not really a true nut, but a drupe.
In young, green coconuts there is a lot of coconut water.
Coconut milk is made from the white flesh.
Coconuts can drift for a long time in the sea and sprout on foreign beaches.

abschnitte.text: Coconut palms need a lot of **warmth** and **sun**. They therefore grow in the **tropics**, often right on sandy beaches. The trunk is slender and often slightly curved. A coconut palm can grow up to about **30 metres** tall, as high as a house with ten storeys. At the very top sit the big, feathery leaves. Below them the coconuts hang in clusters.

For plant scientists the coconut is not a true nut, but a **drupe**, like the cherry or the plum. On the outside it has a thick layer of hard **fibres**. Inside lies the hard brown shell. On it you can see three dark spots, the **“eyes”**. From one of them the new palm grows out. Inside is the white **flesh**.

Coconuts are light and, thanks to their fibres, **waterproof**. If a coconut falls into the sea, it can drift for a long time. If it is washed up on another beach, it can **sprout** there and grow into a new palm. In this way coconut palms have spread to many islands, entirely without the help of humans.

In young, green coconuts there is a lot of clear **coconut water**. You can drink it straight from the nut. In older nuts the flesh becomes thicker. It is grated and pressed, and this makes **coconut milk** for cooking. Dried flesh is called **copra**. From it **coconut oil** is obtained, which is used in the kitchen and in cosmetics.

The fibres of the outer layer are called **coir**. From them people make **ropes**, **brushes** and **doormats**. The leaves too are used, for example for roofs and woven baskets. Because almost everything about it can be used, some people call the coconut palm the “tree of life”.

gewusst: The coconut is called a nut although it is a drupe.
Doormats made of coir lie in the entrances of many Swiss homes too.

teile.einleitung: Maize is one of the most important crops in the world. It comes from the Americas and today is grown almost everywhere, as food for people and as feed for animals.
wichtigste: Maize originally comes from the Americas.
It was first grown in what is now Mexico.
The kernels sit in rows on a cob.
