After the voyages of Columbus, the Spanish brought maize to Europe.
In Switzerland a lot of maize is grown as animal feed.
Maize is used to make polenta, tortillas and popcorn.

abschnitte.text: Maize was first grown in the **Americas**. Thousands of years ago, people in what is now **Mexico** bred maize from a wild grass. For the peoples of Central America it was a staple food. To this day maize is very important in Mexico.

After the voyages of **Columbus**, Spanish sailors brought maize to Europe about 500 years ago. Before that it was unknown here. From Europe it spread further to Africa and Asia. Today, together with wheat and rice, maize is one of the most important cereals in the world.

Maize is a tall grass and can grow more than two metres high. The kernels sit in rows on the **corn cob**. The cob is wrapped in green leaves, the **husks**. At the top of the plant, the male flowers sit as a tassel, and the wind carries their pollen to the cobs.

Cornmeal is boiled to make **polenta**, a porridge that is very popular in **Ticino** and northern Italy. In Mexico, thin flatbreads called **tortillas** are baked from maize flour. Certain maize kernels burst open when heated: inside each kernel there is a little water, which turns to steam. This is how **popcorn** is made.

Maize grows in many Swiss fields. A large part of it is used as **animal feed**. Often the whole plant is chopped up and stored as **silage** for the cows. A smaller part is harvested as grain maize or ends up on the plate as sweetcorn.

gewusst: Popcorn pops because the water in the kernel turns to steam and bursts the hard shell.
Maize descends from a wild grass that looked quite different from a modern corn cob.

teile.einleitung: Seawater is the salty water of the oceans and seas. It covers most of the Earth and differs from the fresh water in our lakes and rivers.
wichtigste: About 71 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered by sea.
About 97 per cent of the water on Earth is salt water.
One litre of seawater contains on average about 35 grams of salt.
The salt comes from rocks on land.
Seawater freezes only at about minus 2 degrees Celsius.
The Baltic Sea is much less salty than other seas.

abschnitte.text: About **71 per cent** of the Earth's surface is sea. That is why the Earth is also called the **blue planet**. Almost all the water on Earth, about **97 per cent**, is salty seawater. Only about 3 per cent is **fresh water**, and a large part of that is frozen as ice. The water in Swiss lakes such as Lake Zurich or Lake Geneva is fresh water.

Seawater contains on average about **3.5 per cent** salt. In one litre that is about **35 grams**, roughly seven teaspoons. Most of it is **common salt**. Not all seas are equally salty. Many rivers carrying fresh water flow into the **Baltic Sea**, so it is much less salty.

Rain dissolves tiny amounts of salt out of **rocks** on land. Rivers carry this salt to the sea. When seawater evaporates, only the water goes into the air, and the salt stays behind. In this way more and more salt has built up in the sea over a very long time.

If you let seawater evaporate in the sun, **salt** is left over. In a **saltworks**, seawater is led into shallow basins. Sun and wind make the water evaporate, and afterwards the salt can be collected. In Switzerland, by contrast, salt is obtained from salt deposits deep underground, for example in the saltworks on the Rhine.

Fresh water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius. The **salt** in seawater makes it freeze only at a lower temperature. Seawater freezes at about **minus 2 degrees** Celsius. That is also why salt is spread on icy roads in winter.

gewusst: One litre of seawater holds about as much salt as seven teaspoons.
Only a small part of the water on Earth is fresh water, and a large part of that is frozen as ice.

teile.einleitung: At about 3,954 metres, Mount Robson is the highest mountain in the Canadian Rocky Mountains. It lies in the province of British Columbia and rises mightily above its surroundings.
wichtigste: Mount Robson is about 3,954 metres high.
It is the highest peak in the Canadian Rocky Mountains.
It lies in British Columbia in Mount Robson Provincial Park.
The mountain towers above its surroundings by almost 3,000 metres.
It is not Canada's highest mountain: Mount Logan in the Yukon is higher.

abschnitte.text: The **Rocky Mountains** are a long mountain range in the west of North America. Their highest peak in Canada is **Mount Robson**, at about 3,954 metres. It lies in the province of **British Columbia**, near the border with Alberta. Because the valley at its foot lies low, the mountain towers above its surroundings by almost 3,000 metres. That is why it looks especially mighty. The highest mountain in all of Canada, however, is **Mount Logan** in the Saint Elias Mountains in the Yukon.

Around the mountain lies **Mount Robson Provincial Park**, one of the oldest parks in British Columbia. There are forests, glaciers, waterfalls and lakes. In the park the **Fraser River**, one of the big rivers of Canada, also rises. A popular hiking trail leads to Berg Lake at the foot of the north face, where ice breaks from the glacier into the lake. Animals such as bears, elk and mountain goats live in the park.

The summit is often wrapped in cloud, and the weather changes quickly. Mount Robson is therefore regarded as a difficult mountain for climbers. The first ascent was made in 1913 by a small group with the mountain guide **Conrad Kain**, who came from Austria. To this day only a few climbers reach the summit.

gewusst: Mount Robson is about 500 metres lower than the Matterhorn, at 4,478 metres.
Because the summit is so often in cloud, many visitors never see the whole mountain.

teile.einleitung: The Mekong is the longest river in Southeast Asia. It begins in the highlands of Tibet and flows through six countries to the sea. For many millions of people it is a lifeline, a road and a source of food all at once.
wichtigste: The Mekong rises in the highlands of Tibet in China.
It flows through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam.
At over 4,000 kilometres, it is the longest river in Southeast Asia.
In southern Vietnam it splits into many arms: the Mekong Delta.
The delta is one of the most important rice-growing areas in the world.
The Mekong giant catfish lives in the Mekong, one of the biggest freshwater fish.

abschnitte.text: The Mekong begins high up in the **highlands of Tibet** in China. From there it flows south through deep gorges. After that it forms the border between **Laos** and **Thailand** over long stretches. Through Cambodia it finally reaches **Vietnam**, where it flows into the South China Sea.

In the south of Laos, the Mekong plunges over many rock steps at the **Khone Falls**. The falls are not especially high, but they are several kilometres wide. This makes them among the widest waterfalls in the world. Ships cannot get past here, which is why the Mekong was never navigable all the way through.

abschnitte.titel: The Delta of the Nine Dragons
abschnitte.text: In the south of Vietnam the river splits into many arms. This area is called the **Mekong Delta**. The Vietnamese call the Mekong there **Cửu Long**, which means “nine dragons”. In the warm, humid delta so much **rice** grows that it is called the rice bowl of Vietnam. At the **floating markets**, traders sell fruit and vegetables directly from their boats.

The Mekong is very rich in fish. The **Mekong giant catfish** lives here and can grow to about 3 metres long. It has become rare today and is strongly endangered. For many families along the river, fishing is the most important source of food.

In China and Laos, several big **dams** that generate electricity have been built. But they change the flow of the water and hold back mud that the fields further down need. Fish, too, often cannot get past the dams any more. The countries along the river therefore discuss together how they want to use and protect the Mekong.

gewusst: In Cambodia, a side arm of the Mekong flows backwards in the rainy season and fills the big lake Tonle Sap.
The Mekong giant catfish is one of the biggest freshwater fish in the world.

teile.einleitung: A climate zone is a large belt around the Earth in which a similar climate prevails everywhere. Because the Sun shines on the Earth more steeply at the Equator than at the poles, it gets colder and colder from the Equator towards the poles. In this way different zones arise, from the hot tropics to the icy polar regions.
wichtigste: The Earth is roughly divided into tropical, subtropical, temperate, subpolar and polar zones.
The tropics lie between the two tropics (Cancer and Capricorn) around the Equator.
The Sahara lies mainly in the subtropics.
Switzerland lies in the temperate zone with four distinct seasons.
In the subpolar zone there is the tundra, a treeless landscape with mosses and lichens.
North of the Arctic Circle you can see the midnight sun in summer.
Climate zones exist in the Northern and the Southern Hemisphere as mirror images.

abschnitte.text: **Climate** is the typical weather of a place over many years. A climate zone groups together areas with similar temperatures and precipitation. The most important reason for the differences is the **angle of incidence** of the Sun’s rays. At the Equator they strike almost vertically, at the poles only at a shallow angle, like a torch shining at a slant onto a table.

The **tropics** lie between the northern and the southern **tropic**, that is, about 23 degrees north and south of the Equator. There it is warm all year, and there are no real seasons such as summer and winter. Near the Equator it rains a great deal, so tropical rainforests grow there. Further from the Equator there are savannas with rainy and dry seasons.

The **subtropics** adjoin the tropics. Many large deserts such as the Sahara lie here, because dry air often sinks there and hardly any clouds form. The subtropics also include the Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers and mild, damp winters. Typical plants are olive trees and lemons.

In the **temperate zone** there are four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. Switzerland, Germany and most of Europe lie in this zone. Typical are deciduous and coniferous forests. Near the sea the winters are milder, and in the interior of the continents the differences between summer and winter are greater.

The **subpolar zone** has short, cool summers and long, cold winters. Here there is the **tundra**, where, because of the cold, no trees grow any more, but only mosses, lichens and small shrubs. The ground is often frozen deep down, which is called permafrost. In the polar zone around the North and South Poles it is icy cold almost all year.

In the mountains too the climate changes: the higher you climb, the colder it gets, by about half a degree to one degree per 100 metres of height. In the Swiss Alps you can therefore experience several **altitudinal zones** on one hike. Below, deciduous trees grow, higher up coniferous forest, then come alpine pastures and finally rock, snow and glaciers. This is similar to a journey from the Equator to the pole.

begriffe.erklaerung: The average weather at a place over many years.
A circle of latitude above which the Sun stands exactly vertically at midday once a year.
A circle of latitude from which there is at least one day a year when it never gets dark and one day when it never gets light.
A cold, treeless landscape with mosses, lichens and small shrubs.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.

gewusst: At the North Pole the Sun shines for half a year in summer without setting.
Even in the middle of the tropics there are glaciers, for example on Kilimanjaro in Africa.
When it is winter in the Northern Hemisphere, it is summer in the Southern Hemisphere.

teile.einleitung: China is the biggest coal producer in the world. In 2023 the country mined about half of all the coal mined worldwide. Coal still supplies the greatest part of China’s electricity, but the country wants to become CO2-neutral by 2060.
wichtigste: In 2023 China mined over 4 billion tonnes of coal, about half of world production.
The most important mining areas are Shanxi Province and Inner Mongolia.
In 2023 about 60 per cent of China’s electricity came from coal.
China is at the same time the biggest importer of coal, mainly from Indonesia.
Coal burning contributed greatly to the smog in China’s cities.
China wants to become CO2-neutral by 2060.

abschnitte.text: **Shanxi** Province in the north is regarded as China’s classic **coal province**. It has huge deposits of hard coal and has lived heavily from mining for decades. The autonomous region of **Inner Mongolia** is the second big mining area, with huge **open-cast mines**. Together the two areas supply over half of Chinese coal. In the south of the country, by contrast, coal plays hardly any part.

The coal is often mined far inland, but it is needed in the big cities on the coast. The **Daqin Railway** connects **Datong** in Shanxi with the port of **Qinhuangdao** on the Bohai Sea. It is regarded as one of the highest-capacity freight railway lines in the world for coal. From there ships carry the coal on to the south. Despite its own production, China also buys a lot of coal abroad, in 2023 mainly in **Indonesia**, Russia, Mongolia and Australia.

China is expanding **wind** and **solar power** faster than any other country. Even so, in 2023 about **60 per cent** of its electricity still came from coal-fired power stations. About twenty years ago it was about 80 per cent. Part of the coal is also converted chemically. In **coal liquefaction**, for example in **Ordos**, diesel and other liquid fuels are made from it. In this way China wants to import less oil, but a lot of CO2 is produced in the process.

Coal-fired power stations and coal heating release **fine dust** and **sulphur dioxide**. In the winter of 2013 the **smog** in Beijing reached extreme values. After that China introduced stricter programmes for clean air. Another problem is **seam fires**: in the **Wuda** area of Inner Mongolia, layers of coal have been burning underground, in part for decades. In the process coal is burned uselessly, and pollutants and CO2 are produced.

President **Xi Jinping** announced in 2020 that China’s CO2 emissions should peak before 2030. By **2060** the country is to become **CO2-neutral**. That means it should emit no more CO2 than is removed from the air again. For this, the use of coal will have to fall sharply over the next decades.

gewusst: China is at the same time the biggest producer and the biggest importer of coal.
Underground coal fires can burn for decades, because they are hard to put out.

teile.einleitung: The Lesser Antilles are a long chain of islands in the Caribbean. They stretch in an arc as far as South America. Many of the islands were formed by volcanoes.
wichtigste: The Lesser Antilles form an island arc in the Caribbean.
They are divided into the Windward Islands and the Leeward Islands.
Trinidad is the biggest island and lies close to Venezuela.
Many islands are volcanic.
The volcanoes form because the Atlantic Plate sinks beneath the Caribbean Plate.

abschnitte.text: The **Lesser Antilles** line up in an **arc** from the north-east of the Caribbean to South America. Geographers call this an **island arc**. The islands include, for example, Guadeloupe, Martinique, Barbados and Grenada. Some are states in their own right, others belong to France, the Netherlands or Great Britain.

The Lesser Antilles are divided into two groups. The eastern islands lie in the **trade wind** and are called the **Windward Islands**. The islands off the coast of **Venezuela**, such as Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao, are called the **Leeward Islands**. The names come from the language of sailors.

The biggest island of the Lesser Antilles is **Trinidad**. It is about 4,800 km² in size and lies only a few kilometres off the coast of South America. Together with the smaller island of **Tobago** it forms the state of Trinidad and Tobago.

At the eastern edge of the Caribbean, **oceanic crust** of the Atlantic sinks beneath the **Caribbean Plate**. In the process **magma** forms deep down and rises. In this way many **volcanic islands** have formed over a long time. Some volcanoes are still active today, for example on Montserrat or under the sea near Grenada.

gewusst: On the Leeward Islands people speak, among other languages, Papiamento, a language of the region’s own.
There are active volcanoes under the sea too, near the Lesser Antilles.

teile.einleitung: A craton is a very old, stable core of a continent. These blocks of rock have hardly changed for billions of years. The parts that are exposed at the surface are called a shield, for example the Canadian Shield.
wichtigste: A craton is a part of the continental crust that has been stable for a very long time.
Many cratons are more than 2.5 billion years old.
The parts of a craton that are exposed at the surface are called a shield.
Well-known examples are the Canadian Shield and the Baltic Shield.
Some of the oldest rocks on Earth are found here.

abschnitte.titel: The old core of the continents
abschnitte.text: The continents are not the same age everywhere. In their middle there are often very old, solid blocks of rock. These are called **cratons**. Many of them formed in the early days of the Earth, more than 2.5 billion years ago. Since then they have hardly been folded or deformed. Mountains usually form at their edges, not in the craton itself. Beneath a craton, the solid rock shell, the **lithosphere**, reaches down particularly deep.

If the old rock of a craton lies open at the surface, it is called a **shield**. A well-known example is the **Canadian Shield** around Hudson Bay. In Europe, the **Baltic Shield** lies in Scandinavia and Finland. If the craton is covered by younger layers of rock, this part is called a **platform**. One example is the East European Platform.

In cratons you can find some of the **oldest rocks** on Earth. The **Acasta Gneiss** in northern Canada is about 4 billion years old. Cratons are also important for raw materials. Some of them contain gold, iron ore and **diamonds**. Diamonds form deep in the Earth's mantle and reach the surface in volcanic pipes made of **kimberlite**.

gewusst: Switzerland has no craton: compared with one, the Alps are a very young mountain range.
The word craton comes from the Greek word for strength.

teile.einleitung: Cuba is an island nation in the Caribbean and the biggest island in that sea. The country is known for old cars, music, sugar cane and its special history.
wichtigste: Cuba is the biggest island in the Caribbean, about 110,000 km² in area.
The island belongs to the Greater Antilles and is the westernmost of them.
Only about 150 kilometres of sea separate Cuba from Florida in the USA.
The capital is Havana, and Spanish is spoken.
A lot of sugar cane is grown in Cuba.
In 1959 the revolution under Fidel Castro won.

abschnitte.titel: The biggest island in the Caribbean
abschnitte.text: Cuba is long and narrow and about **110,000 km²** in area, so it is a good two and a half times as big as Switzerland. The island belongs to the **Greater Antilles**, the big islands in the north of the Caribbean. To the north, only about 150 kilometres away, lies the US state of **Florida**. The capital is **Havana**. The climate is tropically warm.

In 1492 **Christopher Columbus** reached the island. After that, Cuba was a colony of Spain for a long time, which is why people there speak Spanish. In 1959 **Fidel Castro** and his followers overthrew the dictator Batista. After that, Cuba became a **socialist state**, in which only one party governs. In the 1960s the USA imposed a trade ban on Cuba, which still makes many things difficult today.

In the streets of Havana, many old cars from the **1950s** are still on the road. Because new cars are hard to get, they are repaired again and again. A lot of **sugar cane** grows in the fields, and its sweet juice is made into sugar. Cuba is also known for **tobacco** and cigars. People pay with the Cuban **peso**.

Some animals live in Cuba that exist nowhere else. The rare **Cuban crocodile** lives in the wild only on this island and is protected. The national bird, the **tocororo**, has red, white and blue feathers. These are exactly the colours of the **flag**: it shows blue and white stripes and a red triangle with a white star.

gewusst: Cuba is surrounded by numerous smaller islands, and the second biggest is called Isla de la Juventud.
Music styles such as son come from Cuba, and salsa later developed from it.

teile.einleitung: Mumbai is a huge port city on the west coast of India. It is the most important economic and financial centre of the country and the home of the film industry Bollywood. Until 1995 the city was officially called Bombay.
wichtigste: Mumbai was officially called Bombay until 1995.
The city is the capital of the state of Maharashtra in the west of India.
The railway station Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
At the harbour stands the big archway, the Gateway of India.
The dabbawalas deliver thousands of lunches to offices every day.
On the island of Elephanta there are cave temples carved into the rock.

abschnitte.text: Mumbai lies on the **Arabian Sea** and is the capital of the state of **Maharashtra**. The city originally arose on seven islands, which were later joined by land reclamation. In the 17th century the area passed from Portugal to England. Under British rule it grew into an important port city. In 1995 **Bombay** was officially renamed **Mumbai**, after the goddess Mumba Devi.

The station **Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus** was completed in 1888 in Victorian Gothic style and used to be called Victoria Terminus. Since 2004 it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. At the harbour stands the **Gateway of India**, a big archway. It was built to commemorate the visit of the British king George V and was finished in 1924. Very close by lies the well-known Taj Mahal Palace hotel.

The **dabbawalas** are men who deliver thousands of hot lunches every day. They collect the food in tin boxes from families at home. By train, bicycle and on foot, they bring it to the office and in the afternoon take the empty boxes back. Many cannot read, so they mark the boxes with colours and symbols. Their system is world famous because it is very reliable.

Off Mumbai, in the harbour, lies the island of **Elephanta**. It can be reached by boat. On the island there are **cave temples** that were carved into the rock over a thousand years ago. In them stand big sculptures of the Hindu god **Shiva**. The caves are also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Mumbai is the most important **economic centre** of India. The Bombay Stock Exchange, one of the oldest stock exchanges in Asia, is here. Mumbai is also the home of **Bollywood**, the Hindi film industry, which makes a great many films every year. At the same time many people live in simple settlements, the slums. The contrasts between rich and poor are big.

gewusst: Madras, another big Indian city, is today called Chennai.
The suburban trains of Mumbai carry millions of passengers every day.

teile.einleitung: Coral reefs are huge structures in the sea that are built by tiny animals. They grow in warm, shallow water and are full of life. That is why they are often called the rainforests of the sea.
wichtigste: Corals are animals, even if they look like plants or stones.
A single coral animal is called a polyp.
Corals build their hard skeleton from limestone.
Reef-building corals need warm, shallow and bright water.
A ring-shaped reef with a lagoon in the middle is called an atoll.
Coral reefs are called the rainforests of the sea.

abschnitte.text: Corals look like plants or colourful stones. In reality they are small **animals**, more exactly **cnidarians**. A single coral animal is called a **polyp**. It has a soft body and tentacles with which it catches tiny creatures from the water. Many polyps live together in a **colony**. Reef corals form a hard skeleton of **limestone** beneath them.

When polyps die, their limestone skeleton stays behind. New polyps go on growing on it. In this way a whole **reef** forms over a very long time. Reef-building corals need **warm sea water**, so most reefs are found in the **tropics**. They also need a lot of **sunlight**, because algae live in them that make food with light. In deep water it is too dark for that.

A **fringing reef** grows right on the coast. A **barrier reef** lies further out and is separated from the land by a lagoon. The biggest is the **Great Barrier Reef** off Australia. An **atoll** is a ring of coral reefs and small islands. In the middle lies a **lagoon**. Atolls often form around a volcanic island that slowly sinks into the sea.

In coral reefs live a great many different animals: fish, crabs, starfish, mussels, turtles and many more. That is why reefs are called the **rainforests of the sea**. One well-known inhabitant is the colourful **parrotfish**. It has a mouth like a beak and nibbles algae off the corals. The ground-up limestone it excretes as fine white **sand**.

If the water becomes too warm, the corals lose their coloured algae and turn white. This is called **coral bleaching**. If the heat lasts, the corals die. Pollution, overfishing and damage from anchors also threaten the reefs. Many countries therefore protect their reefs in **marine protected areas**.

gewusst: Many dream-white beaches consist to a large extent of sand made by parrotfish.
The Great Barrier Reef is over 2,000 kilometres long and the biggest structure built by living things on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The Mississippi Delta lies in the US state of Louisiana, where the Mississippi flows into the Gulf of Mexico. It consists of marshes, swamps and many river arms. For decades the delta has been losing land to the sea every year.
wichtigste: The delta lies in Louisiana on the Gulf of Mexico.
It formed from mud that the river deposited over thousands of years.
Dams now hold back a lot of sediment.
Levees prevent the river from bringing mud onto the marshes.
At the same time the ground is sinking, and the sea is advancing.

abschnitte.text: A **delta** forms when a river deposits **sediment**, that is, sand and mud, at its mouth. In this way the Mississippi built up a big area of land over thousands of years. As it did so, it changed its course again and again and built new parts of the delta. **Marshes**, swamps and islands formed, where many birds, fish and crabs live.

Today **dams** further upstream catch part of the sediment. High **levees** on the river protect the cities from floods. But they also prevent the river from bringing mud onto the marshes during floods. At the same time the **ground slowly sinks**, and the sea level rises. In this way coastal land is lost every year, several thousand square kilometres since the 1930s.

The marshes slow down **storm surges** during hurricanes and so also protect the city of **New Orleans**. That is why people are trying to save the delta. Part of the river water is to be channelled through openings in the levees so that new land can form. In addition, marshes are being built up again with dredged sand.

gewusst: A large part of New Orleans lies lower than sea level.

teile.einleitung: The sea lamprey is a primitive, fish-like animal with no jaws. In the Great Lakes of North America it became a big problem for fish as an introduced species.
wichtigste: The sea lamprey is a jawless, eel-like animal.
It has a round sucking mouth with horny teeth.
It fastens onto fish and feeds on their blood.
It reached the upper Great Lakes through shipping canals.
There, in the 20th century, the stocks of lake trout almost collapsed.

abschnitte.text: The **sea lamprey** looks like an eel, but it is not a true fish with a jaw. It belongs to the **cyclostomes**, a very old group of animals. Instead of a jaw it has a round **sucking mouth** with many horny teeth. In German it is called “Neunauge” (“nine-eye”) because the gill openings and the eye on the side of the head together look like nine eyes.

Adult sea lampreys are **parasites**. They fasten onto other fish, rasp through the skin and feed on their **blood**. Many fish do not survive this. In the Atlantic, their home, the fish have adapted to these enemies.

abschnitte.titel: A problem in the Great Lakes
abschnitte.text: Through **shipping canals**, sea lampreys reached the upper **Great Lakes** of North America. There they had hardly any natural enemies. In the 20th century the stocks of **lake trout** almost collapsed because of this, and fishing suffered badly too. Since then the USA and Canada have fought the sea lamprey together, among other things with barriers in rivers.

gewusst: The German name “Neunauge” (“nine-eye”) comes from the eye, nostril and seven gill openings on each side, which look like nine eyes.

teile.einleitung: The Korean Peninsula lies in the east of Asia between China and Japan. Since 1945 it has been divided into two states: North Korea and South Korea. The landscape is mostly mountainous.
wichtigste: The peninsula lies between the Yellow Sea in the west and the Sea of Japan in the east.
About 70 per cent of the peninsula is mountainous.
The highest mountain is the volcano Paektusan at about 2,744 metres.
In 1945 Korea was divided at the 38th parallel into a Soviet and an American zone.
The Demilitarised Zone separates the two Koreas over a width of about four kilometres.
Switzerland has monitored the armistice with officers since 1953.
Pyongyang is the capital city of North Korea, and Seoul is the capital city of South Korea.

abschnitte.text: About **70 per cent** of the peninsula consists of **uplands**. People and farming are therefore concentrated on the **plains** in the west and south. The highest mountain is the volcano **Paektusan** at about 2,744 metres. It lies on the border between North Korea and China and has a **crater lake**. Its eruption around the year 946 was one of the strongest of the last millennia.

In the west the peninsula borders the **Yellow Sea**. It lies between Korea and China and is named after the yellow **loess** that rivers carry into it. In the east lies the **Sea of Japan**. In the south the **Korea Strait** separates the peninsula from Japan. In this strait lies the Japanese island of **Tsushima**. Off the south coast lies the island of **Jeju**, the biggest island of South Korea.

From 1910 to 1945 Korea was occupied by **Japan**. After the Second World War the **USA** and the **Soviet Union** agreed to divide Korea at the **38th parallel**. In 1948 two states arose. From 1950 to 1953 the **Korean War** raged. Since then the **Demilitarised Zone** has separated the two Koreas. It is about four kilometres wide and about 250 kilometres long.

**Switzerland** has monitored the armistice together with **Sweden** since 1953. The two neutral countries form the **Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission**. Members of the Swiss Armed Forces are stationed near **Panmunjom** on the demarcation line. They make sure that both sides can stay in conversation with each other.

**Pyongyang**, the capital city of North Korea, lies on both sides of the **Taedong** River, which flows into the Yellow Sea. **Seoul**, the capital city of South Korea, lies on the **Han** River. **Busan** in the south-east is the second biggest city in South Korea. It lies on the Korea Strait opposite Japan, and its **container port** is among the biggest in the world.

gewusst: The Korean script **Hangeul** was specially created in the 15th century under King Sejong so that all people could learn to read.
In the crater lake on Paektusan the border between North Korea and China runs through the middle of the water.

teile.einleitung: The Congo Basin is a huge, flat depression in Central Africa drained by the Congo River and its tributaries. Here grows the second biggest rainforest on Earth. Its forests and peatlands store so much carbon that they are important for the world’s climate.
wichtigste: The catchment area of the Congo covers about 3.7 million square kilometres.
After the Amazon, the Congo has the second biggest water flow in the world.
In the Congo Basin there is a humid, hot tropical climate.
In the Cuvette Centrale lies the biggest tropical peatland on Earth.
Salonga National Park is the biggest protected area in the tropical rainforest of Africa.
Deforestation is the greatest danger to the rainforest.

abschnitte.text: The Congo Basin is a wide, flat **depression** in the middle of Africa. The **Congo** River and its tributaries drain an area of about **3.7 million square kilometres**. At the mouth, on average about 40,000 cubic metres of water per second flow into the sea. Only the **Amazon** carries more water. Because the basin lies north and south of the **Equator**, it is always the rainy season somewhere. In this way the floods of the tributaries balance one another out, and the Congo carries a lot of water all year.

In the Congo Basin it is **warm and humid** all year. Almost every day there can be heavy rain, often in the afternoon. In the **Cuvette Centrale**, the deepest part of the basin, lies the biggest tropical **peatland** on Earth. Peat forms from plant remains that hardly rot in the wet ground. It contains huge amounts of **carbon**. If the peatland were destroyed, this would get into the air as **carbon dioxide**.

In the rainforest the **leopard** hunts monkeys and small antelopes. Tigers, by contrast, live only in Asia and jaguars only in the Americas. There are also gorillas, bonobos, forest elephants and many species of birds. Under the trees grow valuable timbers such as **sapele**, a reddish wood similar to mahogany. It is used for furniture and floors.

Many farming families traditionally practise **shifting cultivation**. They clear a piece of forest and plant it for a few years. When the soil is exhausted, they move on, and the forest slowly grows back. The rivers are important transport routes. **Salonga National Park** in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is about 36,500 square kilometres in size, almost as big as Switzerland. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984 and in many places can be reached only by boat.

Trees and soils take **carbon dioxide** from the air and store it. That is why protecting the Congo Basin is important for the **world’s climate**. The greatest danger is **deforestation**. Trees are felled for valuable timber, and areas are cleared for fields. Roads for logging companies also open up the forest to hunters.

gewusst: Salonga National Park is almost as big as the whole of Switzerland.
The peatland of the Cuvette Centrale was mapped exactly by researchers only in 2017.

teile.einleitung: La Soufrière is an active volcano on the Caribbean island of St Vincent. In April 2021 it erupted explosively, but thanks to an early warning hardly anyone was killed.
wichtigste: La Soufrière lies in the north of the island of St Vincent in the Caribbean.
It is the highest mountain on the island.
In April 2021 the volcano erupted explosively.
The north of the island had been evacuated in good time beforehand.
The ash covered large parts of St Vincent.

abschnitte.text: **La Soufrière** is a **stratovolcano** in the north of the island of **St Vincent**. The island belongs to the country of St Vincent and the Grenadines and lies in the **Lesser Antilles**. The name comes from French and means roughly “sulphur pit”, because the volcano smells of sulphur. It is the highest mountain on the island and has erupted several times before, for example in 1902 and 1979.

At the end of 2020, a new **lava dome** began to grow in the crater. Experts in **volcano monitoring** watched the mountain closely and measured earthquakes and gases. When the signs became threatening, the government called for the north to be **evacuated**. Thousands of people left their homes. On 9 April 2021 the volcano then erupted **explosively** and hurled ash high into the sky.

The **ash** covered large parts of St Vincent with a grey layer. Houses, fields and water pipes were damaged. The wind even carried ash as far as the neighbouring island of **Barbados**. Because people had been warned in time, hardly anyone was killed. The eruption is therefore seen as an example of how important good monitoring is.

gewusst: On several Caribbean islands, volcanoes are called La Soufrière or Soufrière Hills, because they smell of sulphur.

teile.einleitung: The Loop Current is a warm ocean current in the Gulf of Mexico. It is important for the weather in the region, because it can make hurricanes especially strong.
wichtigste: The Loop Current brings warm water from the Caribbean into the Gulf of Mexico.
It flows through the Yucatán Channel between Mexico and Cuba.
It makes a loop in the Gulf, which is where its name comes from.
After that it flows through the Straits of Florida and feeds the Gulf Stream.
Because its layer of warm water reaches deep, hurricanes above it can become stronger.

abschnitte.text: The **Loop Current** begins where warm water from the **Caribbean** flows through the **Yucatán Channel** between Mexico and Cuba into the **Gulf of Mexico**. In the Gulf the current describes an arc, a loop, which is why it is called the Loop Current. Then it leaves the Gulf through the **Straits of Florida**. There it passes into the Florida Current, which later feeds the **Gulf Stream**.

The loop is not always the same size. Sometimes it reaches far north into the Gulf. From time to time, large, warm **eddies** break away from the current and drift slowly west. They, too, contain a lot of warm water.

**Hurricanes** get their energy from warm seawater. Normally a storm stirs up cooler water from the depths and so weakens itself. With the Loop Current, however, the **warm layer** reaches very deep. That is why a storm hardly cools the water and can keep getting stronger. Meteorologists therefore watch the current closely.

gewusst: The Gulf Stream, which the Loop Current helps to feed, also provides a milder climate in Europe.
The warm eddies of the Loop Current can be several hundred kilometres across.

teile.einleitung: Lonesome George was a famous giant tortoise from the Galápagos Islands. He was the last known animal of his subspecies and became a worldwide symbol of the protection of endangered species.
wichtigste: Lonesome George was the last known Pinta Island giant tortoise.
He came from Pinta Island in the Galápagos archipelago.
He lived for many years at a research station on the island of Santa Cruz.
He died in 2012, and with that his subspecies is regarded as extinct.
He became a symbol of species conservation.

abschnitte.text: On the **Galápagos Islands** in the Pacific, which belong to Ecuador, **giant tortoises** live. On almost every larger island there was a subspecies of its own. On the island of **Pinta**, a single male was discovered in 1971. No other animals of his subspecies were found. That is why he was called **Lonesome George**, which means roughly “lonely George” in German.

In the past, sailors caught many giant tortoises as supplies for their voyages. On Pinta, **goats** were also introduced. They ate the plants that the tortoises lived on. In this way the Pinta tortoises gradually disappeared.

abschnitte.titel: A life at the research station
abschnitte.text: Lonesome George was taken to the **Charles Darwin Research Station** on the island of **Santa Cruz**. Many people from all over the world visited him there. In June **2012** he died. With that, the Pinta giant tortoise is regarded as extinct. Lonesome George became a **symbol** of how important it is to protect endangered animals.

gewusst: Giant tortoises on the Galápagos can live to be more than 100 years old.
The Galápagos Islands became famous through the naturalist Charles Darwin.

teile.einleitung: Cobalt is a silvery, shiny metal with the chemical symbol Co. Today it is found mainly in the batteries of mobile phones and electric cars. The greatest part comes from a single country: the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
wichtigste: Cobalt is a chemical element with the symbol Co and atomic number 27.
In 2023 about three quarters of the world’s mined cobalt came from the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The most important mines lie in the Copperbelt in the south of the Congo, around Kolwezi and Lubumbashi.
Cobalt is mostly obtained as a by-product of mining copper and nickel.
A large part is needed for the cathodes of lithium-ion batteries.
The greatest part of the cobalt is refined in China, that is, purified and processed further.
The name comes from the “Kobold”, a goblin-like mountain spirit from old miners’ legends.

abschnitte.text: Cobalt is rarely mined on its own. Mostly it turns up in the mining of **copper** and **nickel**, so it is a **by-product**. The richest deposits lie in the **Central African Copperbelt** in the south of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Towns such as **Kolwezi** and **Lubumbashi** are centres of mining. In 2023 the Congo supplied about three quarters of world production.

In many **lithium-ion batteries** cobalt is found in the **cathode**, one of the two poles of the battery. It makes the cathode more stable and helps to store a lot of energy. Such batteries are found in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars. Because cobalt is expensive and hard to obtain, there are also batteries without cobalt. **Lithium iron phosphate batteries**, **LFP** for short, need neither cobalt nor nickel. They store somewhat less energy, but are used in many electric cars.

Besides large industrial mines, there is **artisanal mining** in the Congo. This is small-scale mining by hand, often with shovels and picks. Thousands of people dig for ore there without protective clothing, some of them children. Dust and deep, unsecured pits are dangerous. These conditions are sharply criticised internationally. Many companies therefore promise to check the origin of their cobalt carefully.

The commodities company **Glencore** has its headquarters in **Baar** in the canton of Zug. In the Congo it operates large copper and cobalt mines, including **Kamoto** and **Mutanda**. This makes Glencore one of the biggest cobalt producers in the world. The ore or an intermediate product is then mostly shipped to **China**. There the greatest part of the world’s cobalt refining takes place.

abschnitte.titel: A metal with a legendary name
abschnitte.text: The name cobalt comes from the German **Kobold**, a goblin-like mountain spirit. In the past miners found an ore that looked like silver ore. When smelted, however, it gave off poisonous **arsenic fumes** and yielded no usable metal. The miners believed that goblins had bewitched the ore. Only the Swedish chemist **Georg Brandt** recognised in the 18th century that it contained a metal of its own.

gewusst: For centuries cobalt has been used to colour glass and porcelain deep blue, and this colour is called **cobalt blue**.
Like iron and nickel, cobalt is magnetic.
Humans too need tiny amounts of cobalt: it is found in **vitamin B12**.

teile.einleitung: Melanesia is a region of islands in the south-western Pacific, north and north-east of Australia. It includes Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji and New Caledonia. The region has a very long history and a huge variety of languages and cultures.
wichtigste: The name Melanesia means “black islands”.
Melanesia includes Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji and New Caledonia.
New Caledonia is a French overseas territory and is rich in nickel.
Vanuatu became independent in 1980, and before that it was called the New Hebrides.
From Melanesia, the Lapita culture settled the distant Pacific.
On the island of Tanna in Vanuatu lies the almost constantly active volcano Yasur.

abschnitte.text: The Greek word **melas** means black. European sailors named the region after the dark skin colour of many of its inhabitants. Melanesia is one of the three big island regions of the Pacific, alongside **Micronesia** and **Polynesia**. The biggest island is New Guinea. In Papua New Guinea alone, several hundred different languages are spoken.

From about 1500 BC the **Lapita culture** spread out from the **Bismarck Archipelago**. It is known for its finely decorated pottery. The Lapita people were the first to settle Fiji, Tonga and Samoa and are regarded as ancestors of the Polynesians. On the Trobriand Islands the researcher **Bronisław Malinowski** described the **Kula ring**: necklaces and armbands travel from island to island, and what matters is prestige and friendship, not profit.

Vanuatu used to be called the **New Hebrides** and was governed jointly by Britain and France. In 1980 Vanuatu became independent. In **New Caledonia** the population voted against independence from France in 2018, 2020 and 2021. The last vote was boycotted by many Kanak, the Indigenous people, so the question remains disputed. On **Bougainville** in Papua New Guinea, about 98 per cent voted for independence in 2019, which now has to be negotiated.

New Caledonia has a large share of the world's known **nickel deposits**. Nickel is needed for stainless steel and batteries. Many islands of Melanesia are volcanic. **Yasur** on the island of Tanna has been almost continuously active for centuries and throws out glowing lava. Visitors can climb to close to the crater rim.

gewusst: Papua New Guinea is one of the countries with the most different languages in the world.
In the New Hebrides there were two administrations and two legal systems side by side.

teile.einleitung: Lithium is a chemical element and the lightest of all metals. It is in great demand today because it is needed for the batteries in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars.
wichtigste: Lithium has the chemical symbol Li and the atomic number 3.
It is the lightest metal and would even float on water.
Lithium reacts with water and is therefore stored under oil.
It is an important material for lithium-ion batteries.
There are large lithium deposits in the Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia.

abschnitte.text: **Lithium** is in third place in the periodic table and belongs to the **alkali metals**. It is silvery, soft and so light that it could float on water: its density is only about **0.53 grams per cubic centimetre**. But lithium reacts with water and air. That is why it is kept under **oil** in the laboratory. The name comes from the Greek word “lithos” for stone.

Today lithium matters most for **lithium-ion batteries**. They are found in mobile phones, laptops, e-bikes and **electric cars**. Because lithium is so light and stores electricity well, these batteries can take in a lot of energy for little weight. That is why demand for lithium has risen sharply in recent years.

Lithium does not occur in a pure form in nature, but in rocks and in salty water. Large deposits lie beneath **salt lakes** in South America. The **Salar de Uyuni** in Bolivia is the biggest salt flat in the world. Beneath its salt crust lies **brine**, that is, salt water with a lot of lithium. In Australia, on the other hand, lithium is mainly obtained from rock.

gewusst: Lithium was discovered in Sweden in 1817.
Lithium colours a flame bright red, which is used in fireworks.

teile.einleitung: Madagascar is a big island in the Indian Ocean off the east coast of Africa. Many animals and plants live on the island that are found nowhere else in the world.
wichtigste: Madagascar is the fourth biggest island in the world.
The capital is called Antananarivo.
The official languages are Malagasy and French.
Lemurs and the fossa live in the wild almost only in Madagascar.
Madagascar is one of the most important countries for vanilla.
Rice is eaten at almost every meal.

abschnitte.text: Only Greenland, New Guinea and Borneo are bigger, which makes **Madagascar** the **fourth biggest island** in the world. It is about fourteen times as big as Switzerland. The capital, **Antananarivo**, lies in the **highlands** in the middle of the island and is the biggest city. Madagascar was a colony of **France** and became independent in 1960. That is why **French** is an official language alongside **Malagasy**.

Many millions of years ago, Madagascar separated from Africa and later from India. Since then the island has been **isolated**. Animals and plants there have evolved separately from the rest of the world. This produced very many species that are found only in Madagascar. They are called **endemic**.

The best-known animals are the **lemurs**. These are relatives of monkeys with big eyes and long tails. In the wild they live only in Madagascar and the nearby Comoros. Their enemy is the **fossa**, a cat-like predator that climbs well. About half of all **chameleon species** live in Madagascar. They can change colour.

Several species of **baobab** grow in Madagascar, in German also called the **monkey-bread tree**. These trees have a very thick trunk in which they store a lot of **water**. Famous is the **Avenue of the Baobabs** in the west of the island, where tall trees stand at the side of the road.

In Madagascar people eat a great deal of **rice**, often three times a day. It is grown in many fields on the island, often on terraces. Madagascar is one of the most important countries for **vanilla**. Much of the vanilla for ice cream and cakes in Switzerland comes from there. Many people in Madagascar are poor, and the forest is threatened by logging.

gewusst: The smallest known lemur, a mouse lemur, weighs only about 30 grams.
In Madagascar there are no wild lions, elephants or giraffes, as there are on the nearby mainland.

teile.einleitung: An avalanche is a large mass of snow that suddenly slides or tumbles down a mountainside. In Switzerland, with its many mountains, avalanches are an important natural hazard, especially for winter sports fans and mountain villages.
wichtigste: An avalanche is snow that breaks loose on a slope and slides or tumbles down into the valley.
Most fatal accidents among skiers and ski tourers are caused by slab avalanches.
Slab avalanches usually release on slopes steeper than about 30 degrees.
The SLF in Davos issues the avalanche bulletin for Switzerland every day in winter.
The European avalanche danger scale has five levels, from low to very high.
People who are buried must be freed within about 15 minutes if possible.
Protection forests hold the snow on the slope and protect many villages.

abschnitte.text: In winter, snow falls in many layers, one on top of another. Some layers are firm, others loose and weak. When a weak layer can no longer bear the weight above it, the snowpack breaks. The trigger can be new snow, wind, warmth or the weight of a person. On steep slopes of about **30 degrees** or more it becomes especially dangerous.

In a **slab avalanche**, a whole layer of snow breaks loose at once, like a big plate. It is usually triggered by the victims themselves and is the most dangerous kind for winter sports fans. A **loose snow avalanche** starts at one point and gets wider and wider as it moves downhill. In a **powder avalanche**, the snow whirls up as a huge cloud and can become very fast. **Wet snow avalanches** often occur in spring, when the snow is heavy and damp.

The **WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF** in Davos observes the snow in the Swiss Alps. In winter it issues the **avalanche bulletin** every day. It states the danger level according to the European **avalanche danger scale**. It has five levels: 1 low, 2 moderate, 3 considerable, 4 high and 5 very high. Many accidents already happen at level 3.

Anyone going off the pistes needs an **avalanche transceiver**. It sends out a radio signal that other devices can locate. A **shovel** and a **probe**, which is used to search for buried people in the snow, are also part of the kit. When someone is buried, every minute counts: in the first 15 minutes or so, most people survive. After that the chances fall quickly, mainly because of a lack of oxygen.

Many mountain villages in Switzerland are protected by a **protection forest**. The trees hold the snow on the slope and slow small avalanches. That is why protection forests are especially protected. In addition there are **avalanche barriers** made of steel or wood and galleries over roads. In the avalanche winter of **1999**, an extreme amount of snow fell in a short time, and people died in Galtür in Austria and in Evolène in the Valais.

gewusst: Powder avalanches can reach speeds of more than 200 kilometres per hour.
The SLF in Davos is one of the best-known avalanche research institutes in the world.

teile.einleitung: Mate is an infusion drink from South America. It is made from the dried leaves of a plant and traditionally drunk through a metal straw.
wichtigste: Mate is a drink made from the dried leaves of the yerba mate shrub.
The plant belongs to the holly family.
Mate is especially popular in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and southern Brazil.
It is drunk through a tube with a strainer, the bombilla.
Mate contains caffeine and has a stimulating effect.

abschnitte.text: Mate is made from the dried and chopped leaves of the **yerba mate shrub**. The plant belongs to the **holly family** and grows in South America. The **Guaraní**, an Indigenous people, were already using the leaves. Mate contains **caffeine** and therefore has a stimulating effect similar to coffee or tea.

Traditionally the leaves are put into a vessel, often a **hollowed-out gourd**. This vessel is itself also called a mate. Then hot, but not boiling, water is poured over them. It is drunk through the **bombilla**, a metal tube with a strainer at the lower end. This keeps the leaves in the vessel.

In **Argentina**, **Uruguay** and **Paraguay**, mate is part of everyday life. Often a vessel is shared in a group: one person keeps topping up the water and passes it on. This is a sign of friendship. In Paraguay mate is also drunk cold, which is called **tereré**.

gewusst: The bombilla is a drinking straw and a strainer in one.
In Uruguay you see many people who take their mate and a thermos flask everywhere with them.

teile.einleitung: Libya is a big country in North Africa on the Mediterranean. Most of the country is desert, but under the ground lie huge amounts of oil.
wichtigste: The capital of Libya is Tripoli, and the second biggest city is Benghazi.
Libya has the biggest known oil reserves in Africa.
From 1911/1912, Libya was a colony of Italy.
Muammar al-Gaddafi ruled from 1969 to 2011.
The “Great Man-Made River” is a huge network of water pipelines.
The Roman ruined city of Leptis Magna lies east of Tripoli.

abschnitte.text: Libya is about forty times as big as Switzerland, but by far the biggest part of it is **Sahara**. Most people live on the **Mediterranean coast**. The capital, **Tripoli**, lies in the north-west and **Benghazi** in the east. Historically, Libya consists of three regions: **Tripolitania** in the west, **Cyrenaica** in the east and the **Fezzan** in the south.

abschnitte.titel: Ancient times and the colonial era
abschnitte.text: On the coast, Phoenicians and Greeks founded cities in ancient times, and later the area belonged to the **Roman Empire**. The ruins of **Leptis Magna** east of Tripoli are very well preserved. The Roman emperor **Septimius Severus** was born there. Later, Libya belonged to the Ottoman Empire for a long time. From 1911/1912, **Italy** conquered the country and made it a colony, until after the Second World War.

**Oil** is Libya's most important raw material. The country has the biggest known oil reserves in Africa. Almost all export income comes from oil and gas. The oil was discovered in the 1950s and has changed the country greatly.

In 1951 Libya became independent, at first as a kingdom. In 1969 **Muammar al-Gaddafi** came to power in a coup and ruled the country as a dictator for more than 40 years. In the **civil war of 2011** he was overthrown and killed. Since then the country has been politically divided, and various groups are fighting for power.

Because there is hardly any rain in Libya, water is very valuable. With the **Great Man-Made River**, a huge network of pipes was built. It brings ancient **groundwater** from depths beneath the Sahara to the cities on the coast. It is one of the biggest water projects in the world.

gewusst: Libya does not have a single river that carries water all year round.
The groundwater beneath the Sahara dates from a time when the area was much wetter.

teile.einleitung: A crater is a round, bowl-shaped hollow in the ground. Many craters sit on top of volcanoes. Others formed when lumps of rock from space struck, as on the Moon.
wichtigste: A crater is a round hollow that looks like a bowl.
On a volcano the crater is the opening at the top from which the lava comes.
A secondary crater can form on the side of a volcano.
If water collects in an old crater, a crater lake forms.
A caldera is a huge, collapsed volcanic basin.
Most craters on the Moon are impact craters.
The Greek word “krater” originally meant a mixing vessel.

abschnitte.text: On a volcano the **crater** is the opening at the top of the mountain. In an eruption the **lava** comes out there, along with ash and gases. Even when a volcano is quiet, **smoke** and **steam** often rise from the crater. Sometimes the magma finds another way and emerges on the side of the mountain. There a **secondary crater** forms.

After a very big eruption the **magma chamber** under the volcano is empty. Then the mountain can **collapse** in on itself. A huge basin forms, the **caldera**. When a volcano is extinct, **rainwater** can collect in the crater. In this way a **crater lake** forms. One example is the crater lake on Paektusan in Korea.

Craters also form when **meteorites** from space crash onto a planet or moon. Such craters are called **impact craters**. On the **Moon** there are countless numbers of them. Because the Moon has no air and no weather, they are preserved for a very long time. On Earth, by contrast, craters are slowly worn away by rain, wind and plants. A well-known impact crater is **Meteor Crater** in Arizona in the USA.

The word **crater** comes from **Greek**. For the ancient Greeks a krater was a large **mixing vessel**. In it wine was mixed with water. Because the opening at the top of a volcano recalls such a big bowl, it was later given the same name.

gewusst: In southern Germany the town of Nördlingen lies in an impact crater, the **Nördlinger Ries**.
On the far side of the Moon there are even more craters than on the side we see.

teile.einleitung: Climate migration means that people leave their homes because of the consequences of climate change. Reasons include droughts, floods or rising sea level. Most of those affected move within their own country.
wichtigste: Most climate migrants move within their own country.
The World Bank report “Groundswell” expects up to 216 million internal climate migrants by 2050.
A distinction is made between sudden events such as storms and slow ones such as desertification.
Lake Chad has shrunk greatly since the 1960s.
In 2023 Tuvalu and Australia concluded the Falepili Union.
In 2020 the UN Human Rights Committee made a landmark decision in the Teitiota case.

abschnitte.text: In **climate migration** people leave their place of residence because their environment gets worse through climate change. There are **sudden events** such as storms and floods, which drive people out at a stroke. But there are also **slow changes** such as **desertification** or salinated soils. Usually several reasons come together, such as poverty or conflict.

Most of those affected move over **short distances**, often to nearby cities. For long journeys many lack money and papers. In **Bangladesh** many people move from coastal and river areas to the capital city **Dhaka**. The World Bank report **“Groundswell”** of 2021 expects, in the worst case, up to **216 million** internal climate migrants by 2050. With rapid climate protection there would be far fewer.

**Lake Chad** in Africa has shrunk greatly since the 1960s. Reasons are **droughts** and the taking of water for irrigation. Many fishers and farmers lost their livelihood and moved away. This also intensified conflicts in the region.

Flat **atolls** in the Pacific are severely threatened by rising sea level. In 2014 **Kiribati** bought about 20 km² of land on the Fijian island of **Vanua Levu**, to secure its food supply and to have room in an emergency. Under the **Falepili Union** of 2023, up to 280 people a year from **Tuvalu** can receive a right of residence in Australia.

Under current law, climate migrants are mostly **not regarded as refugees**. In 2020 the **UN Human Rights Committee** decided in the case of **Ioane Teitiota** from Kiribati. Teitiota did lose against New Zealand. But the Committee stated that life-threatening consequences of climate change can in principle make a **deportation** impermissible.

gewusst: Kiribati owns land on an island of another state, on Vanua Levu in Fiji.
Many atolls in the Pacific lie only a few metres above sea level.

teile.einleitung: Chile is the country that produces the most copper in the world. The big mines lie mainly in the Atacama Desert in the north, one of the driest regions on Earth.
wichtigste: Chile produces around a quarter of the world's copper (as of 2023).
Escondida in the Atacama is regarded as the biggest copper mine in the world by output.
The state-owned company Codelco runs the Chuquicamata mine.
In 1971 the big copper mines were nationalised.
Because water is scarce, desalinated seawater is pumped to the mines.
The ore usually contains less than 1 per cent copper.

abschnitte.text: Chile is the world's **biggest copper producer**. In 2023, around a quarter of the world's copper came from Chile, ahead of Peru and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Most of the mines lie in the **Atacama Desert**. The biggest mine by output is **Escondida**, east of the port city of Antofagasta. Copper is very important for Chile's economy and its exports.

In the past, the big mines mostly belonged to companies from the USA. In 1971 Parliament, under President **Salvador Allende**, voted unanimously to **nationalise** them. That means they became the property of the state. Today the state-owned company **Codelco** runs several big mines, including the famous **Chuquicamata** mine near Calama. Private companies also mine copper.

For a long time Chuquicamata was one of the biggest **open-pit mines** in the world, that is, a huge open hole in the ground. Over time it became so deep that mining became too expensive. Since 2019, Codelco has therefore been mining there **underground**, in tunnels. The ore in Chile's **porphyry deposits** usually contains only about 0.5 to 1 per cent copper. That is why enormous amounts of rock have to be moved.

abschnitte.titel: How the copper gets out of the rock
abschnitte.text: First the ore is ground to a fine powder. Then comes **flotation**: the powder is put into water with chemicals, and air is blown in. The copper minerals stick to the **air bubbles** and rise to the top as foam. This takes a lot of water. Because the Atacama is extremely dry, desalinated **seawater** is pumped through long pipelines to heights of over 3,000 metres.

Copper **conducts electricity** very well. Electric cars, wind turbines, solar power plants and power grids need a lot of it for cables and windings. That is why demand is rising sharply. For Chile this is an opportunity, but mining needs a lot of energy and water and changes the landscape. That is why people argue about how to make it kinder to the environment.

gewusst: The Atacama is the driest desert on Earth that is not in a polar region.
In some parts of the Atacama it has hardly ever rained for many years.

tbp4m6.t: Tipping elements in the Earth’s climate system

teile.einleitung: Tipping elements are parts of the climate system that can tip into a new state at a critical threshold. After that the change reinforces itself. Examples are ice sheets, ocean currents and the Amazon rainforest.
wichtigste: Timothy Lenton and his team coined the term “tipping elements” in 2008.
After the tipping point, a positive, self-reinforcing feedback drives the change.
A collapse of the Atlantic overturning circulation would cool north-western Europe.
The Amazon rainforest could turn into a savanna.
The West Antarctic Ice Sheet lies on rock below sea level.
According to a 2025 report, warm-water coral reefs have passed their tipping point.

abschnitte.text: The British researcher **Timothy Lenton** and his team described in 2008 parts of the climate system that can **tip**. When such an element reaches a critical threshold, the **tipping point**, it changes greatly. A **positive feedback** then reinforces the change by itself. Negative feedbacks, by contrast, would stabilise the system.

Bright ice throws back most of the sunlight, while dark sea water absorbs a lot of it. When sea ice melts, the water warms more, and still more ice melts. This is called the **ice-albedo feedback**. A system that has tipped often returns only at a much lower temperature. This phenomenon is called **hysteresis**.

The **West Antarctic Ice Sheet** is considered especially unstable. It lies on bedrock **below sea level** that gets deeper further inland. Warm sea water can push in under the ice. The **Thwaites Glacier** is often called the “Doomsday Glacier”. It is about as big as Great Britain, and its collapse could raise sea level in the long term by several metres.

The **Atlantic overturning circulation** brings a lot of warmth to the North Atlantic. If it collapsed, it would become markedly colder in **north-western Europe** despite global warming. The **Amazon rainforest** produces part of its own rain through evaporation. Through deforestation and droughts it could change over large areas into a dry **savanna**.

The **Global Tipping Points Report** found in 2025 that **warm-water coral reefs** have already passed their tipping point. Repeated marine heatwaves lead to widespread **coral bleaching**. In it the corals lose their colour and can die. Experts stress that rapid climate protection reduces the risk of further tipping elements.

gewusst: The Thwaites Glacier is roughly as big as Great Britain.
Part of the rain in the Amazon region comes from water that the forest itself evaporates.

teile.einleitung: A multinational company is a firm that operates in several countries, often through its own subsidiaries. Such corporations are very important for the world economy. Switzerland is home to many well-known international corporations.
wichtigste: Multinational or transnational companies have subsidiaries in several countries.
Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey, Novartis in Basel.
Many corporations are organised as a holding company with numerous subsidiaries.
Transfer prices apply to dealings between firms of the same corporation.
Since 2024 a minimum tax of 15 per cent has applied in Switzerland for large corporations.
The OECD has drawn up guidelines for the conduct of multinational companies.

abschnitte.text: A **multinational company**, also called a transnational company or “multinational” for short, produces and sells in several states. To do this it founds or buys **subsidiaries** abroad. Its management usually stays in one home country. When an investor holds at least **10 per cent** of the voting rights in a foreign firm, the OECD speaks of a **direct investment**. From this threshold it is assumed that the investor has lasting influence on the firm.

Although Switzerland is small, many global corporations have their seat here. **Nestlé**, one of the biggest food companies in the world, has its headquarters in **Vevey** on Lake Geneva. The pharmaceutical corporation **Novartis** was formed in 1996 from the merger of the Basel firms **Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz**. Roche in Basel and ABB in Zurich are also internationally active. These firms employ very many people worldwide.

Many corporations are built as a **holding company**. A holding company usually produces nothing itself, but holds and manages stakes in other firms. When subsidiaries of the same corporation charge each other for goods or services, the prices are called **transfer prices**. They can be used to shift profits between countries. That is why tax authorities examine them closely.

Under the leadership of the OECD and G20, many states have agreed on a **minimum tax**. Big corporations with a turnover of at least 750 million euros are to pay tax on their profits of at least **15 per cent**. In Switzerland the people approved a corresponding constitutional amendment in 2023. Since 2024 Switzerland has charged a **top-up tax** if a corporation pays less than 15 per cent.

Whether and how corporations should be liable for human rights and the environment abroad is disputed. In November 2020 Switzerland voted on the **Responsible Business Initiative**. About 50.7 per cent of those voting said yes, but the majority of the cantons rejected it. Because a popular initiative needs **a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons**, it was not adopted. In addition there are the **OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises**. In Switzerland the associated National Contact Point is at SECO, where complaints can be submitted.

gewusst: Some global corporations have a turnover each year that is greater than what whole countries earn.
The Responsible Business Initiative was one of the rare initiatives that won the popular majority and still failed on the cantons' majority.

teile.einleitung: The rare earth metals are a group of 17 chemical elements. They are found in smartphones, electric cars and wind turbines. Despite their name, they are not particularly rare, but they are hard to extract.
wichtigste: The rare earths include 17 metals, among them neodymium, lanthanum and cerium.
They are widespread in the Earth's crust, but rarely concentrated enough to be worth mining.
Neodymium is important for very strong permanent magnets.
Dysprosium makes such magnets more heat-resistant.
China dominates mining and above all processing (as of 2023 and 2024).
Separating them is complicated because the elements are chemically very similar.

abschnitte.text: The **rare earths** include the 15 **lanthanides** as well as **scandium** and **yttrium**, 17 elements in all. Some of them are even more common in the Earth's crust than lead. But almost everywhere they are only thinly spread. Deposits where mining pays off are therefore rare.

The most important is **neodymium**. From neodymium, iron and boron the strongest **permanent magnets** are made. They are found in the electric motors of e-cars and in many **wind turbines**. A little **dysprosium** added stops the magnets losing their strength in heat. Other rare earths are needed for screens, phosphors and catalysts.

**China** produces about two thirds of the world's rare earths (as of 2024). In separation and processing the share is even bigger, at about 90 per cent (as of 2023). The biggest known deposit is called **Bayan Obo** and lies in Inner Mongolia. Many countries, including in Europe, are therefore heavily dependent on China and are looking for other sources.

The lanthanides hardly differ chemically. To separate them, many stages of **liquid-liquid extraction** are needed. This costs a lot of energy and chemicals. The mineral **monazite** often contains the radioactive element **thorium**, whose residues have to be stored safely. That is why research is also being done on **recycling** old devices.

gewusst: Four elements are named after the Swedish village of Ytterby: yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium.
Rare earths were first discovered as oxides, which used to be called “earths”, and that is where the name comes from.

teile.einleitung: Laterite is a red, heavily weathered soil or rock material that forms in the hot, humid tropics. It is rich in iron and aluminium but poor in nutrients for plants.
wichtigste: The name comes from the Latin word for brick.
Laterite forms at high temperatures and with a lot of rainfall over a long time.
Iron and aluminium oxides give it its red colour.
Without a cover of plants, it can harden into a hard crust.
Lateritic soils can hardly store any nutrients.
Bauxite, the raw material for aluminium, forms in a similar way.

abschnitte.text: The name **laterite** comes from the Latin word “later”, which means **brick**. Laterite hardens in the air into a material like brick. In **India** and **South-East Asia** it was therefore cut into blocks and used as a building material. Some old temples were also partly built of laterite.

Laterite forms in the **tropics**, where it is very warm for a long time and rains a lot. The warmth speeds up the **chemical weathering** of the rock. The large amount of seeping water washes out easily dissolved substances such as silica. What remains are the **iron and aluminium oxides**, which dissolve only with difficulty. They give the soil its typical **red colour**. Over millions of years, very deep soils form in this way.

Although lush rainforests grow in the tropics, lateritic soils are not very productive for **farming**. Weathering has washed out most of the nutrients. The typical clay mineral **kaolinite** can hold on to only a few nutrients. Under the international soil classification, many such soils belong to the **Ferralsols**. They cover large parts of the Amazon Basin and Central Africa.

If the forest is cleared, the protective cover of plants is gone. Sun and rain hit the soil directly. Then **hard crusts** of laterite can form. These can hardly be worked any more and make farming very difficult. That is why in the tropics it is hard to get good harvests on cleared land for a long time.

**Bauxite** forms through weathering similar to that of laterite. But it is especially rich in **aluminium**. Bauxite is the most important raw material for making aluminium. This is used, for example, to make drinks cans, window frames and parts of aeroplanes.

gewusst: Many rainforest plants get their nutrients mainly from fallen leaves and not from the deep soil.
The red colour of laterite comes from iron oxide, which is also found in rust.

teile.einleitung: The Mississippi is one of the biggest rivers in the world. It flows right through the USA from north to south and empties into the Gulf of Mexico. Famous stories are set on its banks, and in the past paddle steamers sailed on it.
wichtigste: The Mississippi flows through the USA.
It flows from north to south into the Gulf of Mexico.
Near the mouth lies the city of New Orleans.
In the past, paddle steamers sailed on the river.
The longest tributary is the Missouri.
In the language of the Ojibwe, the name means roughly “great river”.

abschnitte.text: The Mississippi begins in the north of the USA in the state of **Minnesota**. From there it flows almost 3,800 kilometres south. Many rivers flow into it. The longest of them is the **Missouri**, which joins it near **St. Louis**. At the end the Mississippi flows into the **Gulf of Mexico**.

Just before the mouth lies the city of **New Orleans**. It is famous for its **jazz music** and its colourful festivals. Parts of the city lie lower than the river. That is why high **levees** protect the houses from floods.

In the past, many **paddle steamers** sailed on the Mississippi. They are driven by big **paddle wheels** turned by a steam engine. The ships carried people, cotton and other goods up and down the river. Today a few paddle steamers still run for tourists, and big barges carry grain.

The writer **Mark Twain** grew up on the Mississippi and as a young man was a pilot on a steamboat. He wrote “The Adventures of **Tom Sawyer**”. Tom lives in a small town on the river and has many adventures there. His friend **Huckleberry Finn**, in another book, travels down the Mississippi on a raft.

gewusst: The name “Mark Twain” comes from the language of river boatmen and means that the water is two fathoms deep.
The name Mississippi comes from the language of the Ojibwe, an Indigenous people.

teile.einleitung: Condensation is the process in which water vapour becomes liquid water. It happens when moist air cools down. This is how clouds, fog and the droplets on a cold bottle form.
wichtigste: In condensation a gas such as water vapour becomes liquid again.
Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
When moist air cools, the vapour condenses into small droplets.
The temperature at which this happens is called the dew point.
This is how clouds, fog and dew form.
The opposite of condensation is evaporation.

abschnitte.text: In the air there is always some invisible **water vapour**. Warm air can take up a lot of it, and cold air less. When moist air cools, it can no longer hold as much water vapour. The vapour then turns into tiny **water droplets**. This process is called **condensation**. The temperature at which it begins is called the **dew point**.

Warm, moist air rises. Up there it is colder, and the air cools. The water vapour **condenses** on tiny dust particles into droplets. Many billions of such droplets form a **cloud**. When the drops become big and heavy enough, they fall to the Earth as **rain**. Condensation is therefore an important part of the **water cycle**.

**Fog** is a cloud right at the ground. It forms when the air near the ground cools strongly, for example on clear autumn nights. In the Swiss **Central Plateau** a thick blanket of fog often lies for days in autumn and winter. **Dew** forms when water vapour condenses on cool blades of grass. In the morning many droplets then glitter on the meadow.

If you take a cold bottle out of the fridge, it soon gets wet. The water vapour from the air condenses on the cold surface. In a similar way, glasses **mist up** when you come in from the cold into a warm room in winter. The bathroom mirror also mists up after a shower. In the sky you see **contrails** behind aeroplanes. There the water vapour from the exhaust gases condenses and freezes.

In **evaporation** liquid water becomes water vapour. This takes heat. In condensation this heat is released again. This **latent heat of condensation** gives thunderstorms and cyclones a great deal of energy.

gewusst: Without dust particles in the air, cloud droplets would form much less easily.
A cloud can contain hundreds of tonnes of water, although it looks light.

teile.einleitung: A cliff is a steep drop at the coast. It forms when the surf strikes the shore again and again and wears away rock. Famous cliffs are found at Dover, on Rügen and in Normandy.
wichtigste: A cliff is a steep slope on the coast shaped by the surf.
At the foot of the cliff the surf washes out a wave-cut notch.
In front of the cliff a flat wave-cut platform is left behind.
A dead cliff is no longer reached by the surf.
Sea stacks are detached towers of rock in the sea.
The cliffs of Dover and Rügen consist of chalk.

abschnitte.text: A **cliff** forms when the **surf** attacks a coast of rock or loose material. The waves knock rock out at the foot of the slope. In this way an indentation forms, the **wave-cut notch**. When the overhang above becomes too big, it breaks off. The cliff thus retreats step by step.
