Port is on the left and starboard is on the right when you look forward.
The front is the bow, the back is the stern, and the floors are called decks.
Lifeboats on the side can take in everyone on board in an emergency.
On the Rhine, river cruise ships sail from Basel to the North Sea.

abschnitte.text: On a cruise ship there are **cabins** for sleeping, restaurants, swimming pools, theatres and shops. The guests live on board for the whole trip. During the day the ship often docks in a port, and the guests visit the town. At night it sails on to the next destination. The biggest ships have room for several thousand guests and need a large crew to look after them.

Ships have their own words. The left side is called **port**, the right side **starboard**. This way there is no mix-up, no matter which direction someone is looking in. The front part is the **bow**, the back part the **stern**. The floors are called **decks**, and round, watertight windows are called **portholes**.

**Lifeboats** hang on the sides of a cruise ship. In an emergency, everyone can leave the ship in them. That is why there is a **lifeboat drill** at the start of every trip. In it, all the guests learn where their assembly point is and where the life jackets are kept.

Not all cruise ships sail on the sea. **River cruise ships** are long, narrow and low so that they can pass under bridges. Many trips begin in **Basel** on the **Rhine**. The river flows through Germany and France to the Netherlands and the North Sea. Such ships also sail on the Danube or the Nile.

Big cruise ships bring thousands of people into a town all at once. In popular places it then gets very crowded. Many ships burn **heavy fuel oil** and give off a lot of exhaust fumes even in port. That is why there are new solutions: some ports offer **shore power**, so that the engines can be switched off during a stop. Some cities also limit the number of ships.

gewusst: In 2021, Venice banned large cruise ships from sailing through the city centre.
On many big cruise ships, people from dozens of different countries work together.

teile.einleitung: Sea turtles are reptiles that spend almost their whole lives in the sea. There are seven species, and almost all of them are threatened today.
wichtigste: There are seven species of sea turtle.
They are reptiles and breathe air with lungs.
Instead of feet they have broad flippers.
The biggest species is the leatherback turtle, about 2 metres long.
The warmth of the sand decides whether females or males hatch.
They often mistake plastic bags for jellyfish.

abschnitte.text: **Sea turtles** are **reptiles** and breathe with **lungs**. That is why they have to come to the surface to breathe. There are **seven species**, and almost all are threatened. The biggest is the **leatherback turtle**, which grows to about 2 metres long. Its shell is covered not with hard plates but with leathery skin.

Their legs have become broad **flippers**, which they use to swim well. Unlike many land tortoises, sea turtles **cannot pull their head and legs into the shell**. In return, their shell is flat and streamlined. This makes them nimble swimmers that cover long distances through the oceans.

To **lay eggs**, the females come ashore. Many return to the beach where they hatched themselves, often over thousands of kilometres. They dig a hole in the sand and lay their eggs in it. The **warmth of the sand** decides what hatches: if the sand is warmer, more females hatch, and if it is cooler, more males.

The newly hatched turtles dig their way out of the sand. Then they scramble **to the sea** as fast as they can. On the way they are in danger from birds and crabs. Artificial light on beaches can confuse the young, which is why some beaches have rules for lighting.

Sea turtles are endangered by **plastic**. A plastic bag in the water looks like a **jellyfish**, which many turtles like to eat. The plastic can make them ill. Other dangers are fishing nets, built-up beaches and global warming, which makes the sand warmer.

gewusst: Whether a female or a male hatches from an egg depends on the temperature of the sand.
The leatherback turtle has no hard shell, but leathery skin on its back.

teile.einleitung: Mount St Helens is a volcano in the north-west of the USA, in the state of Washington. On 18 May 1980 it erupted with enormous force. It was the most destructive volcanic eruption in the history of the USA.
wichtigste: Mount St Helens belongs to the Cascade Range, a series of volcanoes in the west of North America.
The big eruption began on 18 May 1980 at 8.32 a.m. local time.
A huge landslide of the north flank opened the eruption.
57 people lost their lives.
The mountain became about 400 metres lower.
Since 1982 the area has been a National Volcanic Monument.

abschnitte.titel: A volcano in the Cascade Range
abschnitte.text: The **Cascade Range** stretches from northern California to British Columbia in Canada. It consists of **stratovolcanoes** such as Mount Rainier, Mount Hood and Mount St Helens. These volcanoes form because a plate of the sea floor dives under the continent. Before 1980, Mount St Helens was a beautiful, cone-shaped mountain with snow on its summit, about 2,950 metres high. At its foot lay **Spirit Lake**.

In March 1980 earthquakes and smaller explosions began. Magma pushed into the mountain without reaching the surface. This hidden dome is called a **cryptodome**. It made the north flank swell by up to 1.5 metres a day. The authorities set up **exclusion zones** so that nobody stayed close to the mountain.

On Sunday morning at 8.32 a.m., an earthquake of magnitude 5.1 set off a huge **landslide**. It was the biggest landslide in recorded history. This suddenly released the pressure on the magma, and it exploded **sideways**. A column of ash rose about 24 kilometres high. About one cubic kilometre of material was thrown out, which on the **Volcanic Explosivity Index** corresponds to level VEI 5.

Thanks to the exclusion zones the number of victims was comparatively small, but still **57 people** died. Among them was the volcanologist **David A. Johnston**, who was watching the mountain from a post about 10 kilometres to the north. He still reported by radio, “Vancouver! Vancouver! This is it!” The lodge owner Harry R. Truman, who did not want to leave his home at Spirit Lake, also lost his life. Forests were flattened over large areas, and afterwards the summit was only about 2,550 metres high, with a horseshoe-shaped crater.

In 1982 President Ronald Reagan signed the law creating the **Mount St. Helens National Volcanic Monument**. In this protected area, experts study how plants and animals resettle the destroyed land. Soon the first flowers were growing on the ash. In the crater a new lava dome grew later. The volcano is still closely monitored today.

gewusst: Ash from the eruption fell in several states of the USA.
Mount St Helens is one of the best-studied volcanoes in the world.

teile.einleitung: The legend is the key to a map. It shows what the colours, lines and symbols on the map mean, and so helps you to read a map correctly.
wichtigste: The legend explains the colours, lines and signs of a map.
The simplified map signs are called symbols.
Lakes and rivers are almost always blue on maps.
On Swiss national maps, woods are green areas.
Borders are often drawn with dash-dot lines.
Every map has its own signs, so you read the legend first.

abschnitte.text: A map shows the world greatly reduced and simplified. That is why things such as houses, roads or woods are shown with signs. The **legend** explains these signs. It is also called the **key**. Without a legend you would have to guess what the colours and symbols mean.

The fixed map signs are called **symbols**. There are, for example, signs for a church, a railway station or a viewpoint. Some symbols are little pictures, others are lines or areas. On overview maps, **places** are often drawn as dots or circles, and bigger circles usually stand for bigger cities.

Many colours have become standard. **Bodies of water** such as lakes and rivers are almost always **blue**. On the **national maps of swisstopo**, the Federal Office of Topography, woods are **green areas**. Height maps often show low land as green and high land as brown or white. Exactly which colour means what is always stated in the legend.

Lines, too, have different meanings. Roads, railway lines and paths are drawn differently. The **borders** of countries or cantons are often drawn with **dash-dot lines**. There is, however, no single sign language for maps that applies all over the world. That is why it is important to look at the legend first on every new map.

gewusst: The word “legend” comes from the Latin “legenda” and means “that which is to be read”.
Swiss national maps are regarded internationally as especially accurate and beautifully drawn.

teile.einleitung: The Missouri River is the longest tributary of the Mississippi. It rises in the Rocky Mountains in the state of Montana and flows right across the Great Plains. Just above St. Louis it joins the Mississippi.
wichtigste: The Missouri is the longest tributary of the Mississippi.
It is even longer than the Mississippi above the confluence.
It forms in Montana from three headwater rivers.
It joins the Mississippi just above St. Louis.
Together, the Missouri and the Mississippi form one of the longest river systems in the world.

abschnitte.text: The Missouri forms in **Montana**, where three rivers come together. From there it flows north and east through the wide **Great Plains**. At about 3,700 kilometres, it is longer than the Mississippi above the confluence. Together, the **Missouri** and the **Mississippi** form one of the longest river systems in the world.

The Missouri carries a great deal of mud and is therefore often brown. That is why it has the nickname **Big Muddy**. Today big **dams** hold the river back into long lakes. They supply electricity and water for the fields, and protect against floods.

From 1804 to 1806, **Meriwether Lewis** and **William Clark** travelled up the Missouri with a group. They were to explore the west of North America and find a route to the Pacific. They were helped by the Shoshone woman **Sacagawea**. The expedition is regarded as one of the most famous journeys of exploration in the USA.

gewusst: The state of Missouri, too, is named after the river.

teile.einleitung: The Mercator projection is one of the best-known ways of drawing the round Earth on a flat map. It comes from Gerhard Mercator in 1569 and was very useful for sailing. But it shows countries near the poles far too big.
wichtigste: Gerhard Mercator published his world map in 1569 in Duisburg.
The projection is conformal: angles and small shapes stay correct.
A constant compass course appears on the map as a straight line.
Towards the poles, areas are greatly enlarged.
The poles themselves cannot be shown.
Many online map services use the variant Web Mercator.

abschnitte.text: **Gerhard Mercator** was a cartographer from Flanders who lived in **Duisburg**. In 1569 he published a big world map for sailing. Its advantage: lines that cut all the meridians at the same angle are called **rhumb lines**, and on the map they are straight. A sailor could therefore draw a line with a ruler, read off the angle and hold this course with the **compass**.

In this projection you imagine a **cylinder** laid around the Earth. The map is **conformal**: angles and small shapes are right. In return, the scale gets bigger and bigger towards the pole. At 60 degrees latitude, lengths are twice as big as at the equator, so areas are four times as big. The **poles** would lie infinitely far away, which is why Mercator maps usually end at about 80 to 85 degrees latitude.

On the Mercator map, **Greenland** looks about as big as **Africa**. In reality Africa measures about 30 million square kilometres, and Greenland only about 2.2 million. So Africa is about **14 times bigger**. Europe and North America, too, appear bigger than they are. That is why there are other maps, such as **equal-area** projections, which show the sizes correctly but distort the shapes.

Many **online map services** use the **Web Mercator projection**, also called pseudo-Mercator. It is easy to cut into square tiles. When you zoom in, streets and houses keep their correct shape. The national maps of Switzerland, too, are based on an oblique conformal cylindrical projection, a close relative of the Mercator projection.

gewusst: Every flat world map distorts something: a sphere can never be flattened into a plane without errors.
Gerhard Mercator also made the word “atlas” popular for a collection of maps.

teile.einleitung: The sea level is rising because the Earth is getting warmer. There are two main reasons: ice on land is melting, and warmer seawater expands.
wichtigste: According to the IPCC, the mean sea level rose by about 20 centimetres from 1901 to 2018.
From 2006 to 2018 it rose on average by about 3.7 millimetres a year.
The main causes are melting land ice and the thermal expansion of the water.
Melting sea ice hardly raises the sea level at all.
Since 1993 the sea level has been measured by satellites.
A higher sea level leads to more frequent flooding on coasts.

abschnitte.titel: How much is the sea rising?
abschnitte.text: The **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)** estimates that the mean sea level rose by about **20 centimetres** from 1901 to 2018. The rise is getting faster: at the start of the 20th century it was about 1.3 millimetres a year. From 2006 to 2018 it was on average about **3.7 millimetres** a year. Since **1993** this has been measured by **satellite altimetry**: satellites such as TOPEX/Poseidon use radar to measure the distance to the sea surface.

**Glaciers** and **ice sheets** on land, for example in Greenland and Antarctica, release meltwater into the sea. This water was not in the ocean before. The Antarctic ice sheet is the biggest store of ice on Earth. If it melted completely, the sea level would rise by about **58 metres**. The melting of glaciers in the Alps also contributes a small part.

Water expands when it gets warmer. This is called **thermal expansion**. The oceans absorb more than 90 per cent of the extra heat caused by climate change. That is why the sea level rises noticeably from this alone. Along with the melting of land ice, it is the most important reason for the rise.

When **sea ice** melts, the sea level hardly rises at all. This is because of **Archimedes' principle**: floating ice displaces exactly as much water as it weighs. When it melts, it just fills this space. You can try this with ice cubes in a glass. Only ice lying on **land** makes the sea rise.

With a higher sea level, **storm surges** reach further inland, and there is more frequent flooding. In addition, **salt water** can seep into the groundwater. The sea does not rise equally strongly everywhere. On some coasts of **Scandinavia** the sea level is even falling, because the land has been rising since the Ice Age. In the Gulf of Bothnia it rises by almost a centimetre a year.

gewusst: A melting ice cube does not make a full glass of water overflow, just as sea ice hardly makes the sea rise.
Parts of Scandinavia are still rising today because the heavy ice sheet of the Ice Age has disappeared.

teile.einleitung: At a convergent plate boundary two plates of the Earth move towards each other. Often one plate dives beneath the other, or two continents collide. This produces deep-sea trenches, volcanoes, earthquakes and high mountain ranges such as the Andes, the Himalayas and the Alps.
wichtigste: At convergent plate boundaries two plates move towards each other.
The denser oceanic plate dives beneath the lighter one, which is called subduction.
In front of every subduction zone lies a deep-sea trench, and the deepest is the Mariana Trench.
Water from the sinking plate makes the mantle above it melt, and so volcanoes form.
When an oceanic plate dives beneath an oceanic plate, a volcanic island arc forms.
When two continents collide, mountain ranges such as the Himalayas or the Alps fold up.
Slab pull is regarded as the most important driving force of plate tectonics.

abschnitte.text: When an **oceanic** plate meets a **continental** one, the oceanic one dives down. It consists mainly of **basalt** and has a higher **density** than the lighter continental crust. That is why it sinks into the **Earth’s mantle**. This process is called **subduction**. The cold, heavy plate pulls the rest of the plate along behind it. This **slab pull** is regarded as the most important driving force of plate movement.

Where the plate bends downwards, a long, very deep **deep-sea trench** forms on the sea floor. The deepest is the **Mariana Trench** in the Pacific. Its **Challenger Deep** lies almost 11,000 metres below sea level. Sediments on the sinking plate are scraped off at the upper plate and stacked in a wedge shape. This body is called an **accretionary wedge**. In this way the edge of the continent grows over time.

The sinking plate releases **water** at depth. It rises into the mantle above and there lowers the **melting point** of the rock. In this way **magma** forms, which rises and builds volcanoes. On the west coast of South America, the volcanoes of the **Andes** formed like this. When an oceanic plate dives beneath another oceanic plate, an arc-shaped chain of volcanic islands forms, an **island arc**. Examples are the **Marianas** and the **Lesser Antilles**.

At subduction zones there are many and often very strong **earthquakes**. Their foci follow the sinking plate obliquely downwards, to depths of about 700 kilometres. This zone is called the **Wadati-Benioff zone**, after the researchers Kiyoo Wadati and Hugo Benioff. At depth, under high pressure and at a relatively low temperature, special rocks form. One example is **blueschist**, whose colour comes from the mineral **glaucophane**.

Continental crust is too light to dive deep. When two **continents** collide, the rock is compressed, folded and pushed on top of itself. This is how the **Himalayas** formed, when India collided with Asia. The **Alps** also formed in this way: the African Plate and smaller plates moved towards Europe. That is why in the Swiss Alps you find rocks that once lay on the sea floor.

gewusst: The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is high.
Around the Pacific there are so many subduction zones that people speak of the **Pacific Ring of Fire**.

teile.einleitung: There are rivers on every inhabited continent. The longest of them flow for thousands of kilometres, through many countries or right across a whole continent to the sea.
wichtigste: The Nile and the Amazon are the longest rivers on Earth.
At about 6,300 km, the Yangtze in China is the longest river in Asia.
At about 6,000 km, the Mississippi-Missouri system is the longest in North America.
In Europe the Volga is the longest, followed by the Danube.
The Loire is the longest river in France.
The Ob, Yenisei and Lena flow into the Arctic Ocean.

abschnitte.text: The two longest rivers in the world are the **Nile** in Africa and the **Amazon** in South America. Which one is longer depends on where you measure the source. In third place comes the **Yangtze**, at about 6,300 km. It is the longest river in **Asia** and flows only through **China**.

If you measure the **Mississippi** together with its long headwater, the **Missouri**, the total comes to about 6,000 km. This river system is the longest in **North America** and flows into the Gulf of Mexico. The longest river in **Canada** is the **Mackenzie**. It flows about 1,700 km north from Great Slave Lake to the Arctic Ocean. With its headwaters, the system is more than 4,000 km long.

The longest river in Europe is the **Volga** in Russia. In second place comes the **Danube**, at about 2,850 km. It flows through ten countries and into the **Black Sea**. The longest river in **France** is the **Loire**, at about 1,000 km. It flows entirely within France and enters the Atlantic at Saint-Nazaire. The **Rhine**, which rises in Switzerland, is about 1,230 km long.

Three huge rivers flow through **Siberia**: the **Ob**, the **Yenisei** and the **Lena**. They flow from south to north and enter the **Arctic Ocean**. For many months of the year they are frozen. In spring, the ice in the south thaws earlier than in the north, so there are often ice jams and floods.

gewusst: The Danube flows through more countries than any other river in the world.
The Rhine and the Rhône both rise in the Gotthard region of Switzerland, not far from each other.

teile.einleitung: The Colosseum in Rome is the biggest amphitheatre that the ancient Romans built. Nearly 2,000 years ago tens of thousands of people gathered here for gladiator fights and animal hunts. Today it is one of the most famous buildings in the world.
wichtigste: The Colosseum stands in Rome and was inaugurated in AD 80.
It had room for about 50,000 spectators and had 80 entrances.
The outer wall is made of travertine, a light limestone.
The name probably comes from a giant statue of Emperor Nero, the “colossus”.
Earthquakes and stone robbing destroyed part of the outer wall.
In 2007 the Colosseum was voted one of the new seven wonders of the world.

abschnitte.text: Emperor **Vespasian** had the Colosseum built around AD 72. His son **Titus** inaugurated it in AD 80. Its real name is the **Amphitheatrum Flavium**, after the imperial family of the Flavians. The name Colosseum probably comes from a giant statue, a **“colossus”** of Emperor **Nero**, that stood next to it. The outer wall is made of **travertine**, a light limestone from near Tivoli. The blocks were held together with iron clamps.

All round there were **80 entrances** with arches. In this way the many spectators could get in and out quickly. Who sat where depended on rank in society. The important people sat at the bottom, close to the arena. Right at the top sat the **poorer people**. Against sun and rain a huge awning could be stretched over the seating.

In the Colosseum **gladiator fights** and hunts of wild animals took place. The floor of the arena was covered with **sand** so that the fighters did not slip. The Latin word **“arena”** means sand. Under the floor lay a maze of passages and rooms, the **hypogeum**. There animals and fighters waited, and by lifts they came up into the arena.

After the end of the Roman Empire the Colosseum was no longer used for games. **Earthquakes** brought parts of the wall down. Later people took the stones to build other buildings in Rome. That is why part of the outer wall is missing today. What is left is carefully looked after and restored.

The Colosseum is one of the most visited buildings in Italy. In 2007, in a worldwide vote, it was chosen as one of the **new seven wonders of the world**. On **Good Friday** a **Way of the Cross** is traditionally prayed at the Colosseum, usually together with the Pope. Italy also shows the Colosseum on its **5-cent coin**.

gewusst: Under the arena floor there were lifts with which animals could suddenly appear in the arena.
The Colosseum is about 48 metres high, about as high as a house with 15 storeys.
